Question: How long (roughly) would it take a Cessna 172 to fly 400 miles, and how many if any fuel stops?
Answer: Depends on winds aloft and a few other factors. But from previous experience, I’ve flown this profile a few times in a Cessna 172 and similar airplanes I flew from KPVU to KAPA in a C172 which was around 400 nm when taking into account deviations around mountains and weather. The outbound leg was 3 hours and 40 minutes including taxiing, and the inbound leg was 4 hours and 10 minutes. For that flight, I cruised at around 125 knots, at altitudes ranging from 11–14,000 feet. I’ve also flown from U42 (near Salt Lake) to Cheyenne Wyoming in a PA-28–200R (Arrow). That flight was a similar distance and took me just over 3 hours and 30 minutes. I was a little faster because I had a retractable gear plane and a 200HP engine, vs just 180HP and fixed gear for the other flight. I cruised at 11,000 feet for that flight, at around 160 knots true airspeed. An even longer flight in that same plane was my flight from U42 to Falcon Field, near Mesa Arizona. That flight was 500nm, and took me just under 4 hours including taxi. The return was around the same. My numbers were around the same as my Cheyenne flight. Best part of those flights were the view. On my flight back from Falcon Field, I caught the Grand Canyon during sunset. On my flight to Colorado, I got a great view of the Rockies during winter. Weather was nice too. It was a high pressure system day, which meant clear skies and light winds. The perfect kind of day for that type of flight! Here are some pictures from my Falcon Field flight. How beautiful it was!

Question: Why do so many pros use irons off the tee on a par 4 hole?
Answer: I’ll hit an iron off the tee when hitting driver or a fairway wood brings serious trouble into play, such as OB or water. Of course, this is not always the case. However, many times it can be a necessity to hit the iron off the tee on a tight hole like that. With my driver, I average somewhere in the range of 320–330 yards with a good hit. This is great for long, wide open holes. But if the fairway curves, or narrows, then hitting the driver may not always be a good option. Most pros and good amateurs will have a typical dispersion of about 60–75 yards off the tee with their driver. This is true for me as well. As such, any tee shot where penalty strokes are possible with a mishit within that margin will be one where I likely hit iron (either a 2 or 4 iron) off the tee. On a 420 yard hole, with a 250 yard tee shot (around the distance my 2 iron tee shot goes), I’ll have around 170 yards left, which is in between an 8 or 9 iron for me. Still a short iron that I can hit close

Question: Why do professional golfers claim that it is better to miss the hole on the high side, when it is already understood that the ball missed the hole?
Answer: Two reasons. First is that, as other posters have said, missing on the high side gives gravity a chance to knock the ball in the hole. Greens, even the best ones, are imperfect, and many a time, I've hit a putt that I thought had too much break, but the imperfections of the greens knocks the ball back on line and into the hole. Yes, I've had this happen even on greens running 14 on the stimp. The second reason, is that a putt missed on the high side will end up closer than a putt missed on the low side. Again, this is physics. When you hit a putt that travels upslope of where it is supposed to go, it is actually traveling uphill for a little bit. This of course makes the ball roll less than a putt hit with equal speed missed on the low side. During a practice round for the 2014 USGA State Team Championship at French Lick in Indiana (very fast 12+, and undulating greens), I demonstrated this concept when I hit two 20 footers of equal speed at a hole that was breaking about 3 feet right to left. The putt upslope, I deliberately aimed about a foot too much break, and the other one I aimed a foot too little. The result was the putt with too much break ended up about 6 inches right of the hole and a little past, whereas the one with too little rolled off the green after gravity took it down the hill! That was a great visual to me to illustrate this principle. Play more break, especially when the greens are fast and slopey! Your score will thank you

Question: Which known exoplanet is furthest from its sun and still in the Goldilocks region?
Answer: Meet the planet Nu Ophiuchi c. Orbiting a K0III class giant star 3 times the mass of the Sun and 121 times brighter, the gas giant receives slightly more solar radiation than Venus does, despite residing at a grand distance of 6.1 AUs (1 AU = Earth-Sun distance). Orbiting nearly 20 percent farther than Jupiter does our Sun, Nu Oph c would probably be about as close to its star as a planet could get before being considered “too hot” to live on. Assuming a Jupiter-like albedo of 0.52, cloud top temperatures would roughly be the equivalent of summer in Las Vegas, ranging from around 300–320 Kelvins. Not exactly pleasant by any means, but you could make it work if you needed to. I should note that at 24.5 Jupiter masses, you probably wouldn’t want to live here anyways. Minus the issues of finding solid ground to stand on, Nu Oph c could even rightfully be considered a brown dwarf, and almost certainly still be glowing from the heat of its formation, which for Nu Oph c and its inner companion, happened around 330 million years ago. Comparable brown dwarf and massive planets of similar ages all range in temperatures between 800–1300K. The only reason this planet actually qualifies as an answer to this question owes to its formation in a disk like a planet. An inner companion at 22.5 Jupiter masses also orbits the giant star at 1.9 AUs, completing 6 orbits for every 1 orbit the outer planet does. Here is a paper describing exactly how that works, if you’re so inclined to read it. The Extrasolar Planet Encyclopaedia A satellite orbiting this planet may fare better. Now, I’m no astrobiologist, but the Jedi in me postulates that a similarly sized satellite may end up looking something like this. Tatooine’s stellar flux is probably somewhat similar to a possible satellite of Nu Oph c, and although there is only one Sun to cover the sky, the landscape may look similar. The only difference would be a deep red looking gas giant hanging over the sky. Could I picture a sand-hating Jedi living on a moon of this planet? Admittedly not. But truth is sometimes stranger than fiction. And you really never know sometimes.

Question: What were some of the most famous examples of heroism in history?
Answer: Ensign Blair’s prayer that saved a ship from capsizing during a typhoon in the Korean War. As the story goes, Ensign Frank Blair was serving on a ship stationed in Japan that had gotten dangerously close to the eye of a typhoon ravaging the coast of Korea. With only two of the three engines working, one of them on half power at that, and a crack in the centerline of the ship reported, the ship was in dire straits. As he was finishing up his night watch and preparing for bed, the captain, knowing Blair was a devout Christian and member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, asked Blair to pray for the survival of the ship and its crew. As the winds were picking up and the waves were getting dangerously close to capsizing the ship, this was a reasonable request by the captain who needed all the help he could get. Blair agreed to pray for the ship and began to do so. As Blair started to pray, he implored with the Lord of there was something he could do to ensure the survival of the ship. Three times he prayed deeply. On the third time going through the prayer, Blair had a distinct impression to do one more sweep on the boat deck, despite the winds and rain threatening to throw him into the sea at a whim’s notice. As Blair walked on the boat deck, struggling to maintain balance, he noticed one of the ship’s three propellers straining dangerously as it rose above the water. Realizing it would probably fail too at this rate, Blair informed the captain that he needed to slow down the engine, contrary to what the ship’s engineer had just told him. While the captain expressed his doubts, he nevertheless followed Ensign Blair’s advice and slowed the engine down. By dawn, the storm had passed, but less than two hours later, the ship’s one good engine failed as well, leaving the ship to limp home on half an engine’s power. If Ensign Blair prayed and told the captain to slow down the remaining good engine, it would likely have failed during the storm. The ship would have capsized, and all would likely have been lost. In the act of praying for his ship’s safety, Ensign Blair managed to find a solution and save the ship from certain doom.

As someone who didn’t have the Gospel growing up, it helps so many lifelong members rethink and be grateful for what they have. I definitely echo the sentiment some other posters have said about converts being mini-celebrities. For me, I will literally be walking through campus, and a friend of a friend will congratulate me on my baptism. It’s pretty neat. The only downside is that I have to work extra hard not to get too prideful, for fear of becoming like a Nephiite. There is no way to describe just how the room fills with the Spirit so much as when I am attending a class at BYU. Sometimes, I find myself just marveling that everyone in the room knows the same truths that I do of the Gospel. It is definitely an experience that one would classify as priceless. To go from zero to total immersion, especially in something as awesome as the Church is an experience I wouldn’t trade for the world. Now, obviously there are still difficult times. Classes and tests at BYU can be notoriously difficult, especially accounting 200 or econ 110. But would I recommend a recent convert come to BYU? Absolutely. When I was baptized, I was still trying to find my way. But being at BYU helped with that so much. It is the best new member lesson you could possibly ask for. Eventually, I’m sure the novelties of being a new member will wear off. There will come a time when I’m just another face in the House of Israel. But being a convert here is an experience that will stick with me for life. They’re not kidding when they say BYU is the Lord’s university. I truly believe that, from my experience here. For a new member, this school is the best place you can be if you want to learn more about your faith and be in a place with people who will appreciate your story. So the TLDR version for a convert at BYU? 10/10. Highly recommend. Just my two cents.

Question: If there was ever a planet that had at least winters much longer than that of the Earth and summers shorter, what would the planet's axial tilt be?
Answer: Such a planet would likely have an extremely elliptical orbit relative to the Earth rather than a strange axial tilt. Very long winters and short summers is consistent with the planet’s orbit looking somewhat like this. The above shows the orbit of eccentric Jupiter 16 Cygni Bb, a planet notorious for having extremely long winters and extremely short summers. Note how far away the planet is from the Sun at its furthest point in comparison to the orbits of the Solar System planets. The reason the winters last so long is due to two factors. Number one, the planet is travelling slower. If you’ve ever thrown a ball into the sky only to watch it slow down, then fall back to Earth, you’re witnessing the same effect. Two, there is also more space to cover. Kepler’s second law states that a line between the sun and the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times. With so much more area to cover at the far end of its orbit, it would make sense that it takes so long to get through the winter. If superimposed into our Solar System, 16 Cygni Bb’s orbit would take it well into the asteroid belt during its winters. Temperatures dipping well into the -100s would be fairly common for the better part of 17 months. As the planet makes its way around the furthest point in its orbit, it will begin to fall back towards the star, moving faster and faster, until the freezing temperatures are replaced by a relatively balmy spring, then a broiling summer as the planet swings itself well into the inner Solar System, almost as close as Mercury is to the Sun. While this summer period would only last a month or 2, the temperatures would easily reach over 200+ celsius. All too soon, the added momentum from the close approach to the Sun will slingshot the planet back into space, headed for yet another long winter. As it turns out, truth is often stranger than fiction. The world that you mentioned actually does exist. Such is the wonder of our Universe.

Question: Why shouldn't you inflate your life jacket before leaving the plane?
Answer: Inflating your life jacket before leaving the plane is a recipe to drown. Let’s remember that the life-jacket is designed to make you float. Now, this is all fine and what you want it to do for you when outside the plane and floating on the ocean. But if the cabin fills with water? It’ll still have you float, but instead of floating to safety, you’ll float to the top of the cabin, trapped and unable to swim out the exit doors to safety. Ethiopian Airlines Flight 961 is a textbook example of the above-mentioned scenario. After being hijacked, the aircraft ran out of fuel and ditched in the Indian Ocean near the Comoros Islands. But despite surviving the initial crash, many passengers subsequently drowned because they’d inflated their life jackets and were unable to exit the aircraft after it filled with water. While you may correctly point out that the Ethiopian crew had the extreme disadvantage of fighting terrorists in the cockpit at the time of the landing, even the most picture-perfect ditching involves at least some form of water entering the cabin. The odds of landing a commercial jet on the water without any damage to the hull are almost zero. See the diagram below? In the real world, such a ditching may be a fairy-tale reserved for the absolute best-case scenarios. And even if you were able to ditch so perfectly where the hull remained 100 percent intact, the simple act of opening the emergency exit doors would let water into the cabin. If you were the first to get out, again it’s no big deal, but imagine if you were last to exit on an A380 or 777 with 400 other terrified people? Not ideal. Keeping your life jackets uninflated allows you to be able to escape the cabin even if water fills it all the way to the top. While a ditching is indeed unlikely, doing as such may save your life when the crap hits the fan.

Question: Where is the shortest day on the planet?

Question: If you were notified that a giant Tsunami was going to hit your area in 30 minutes, what would you do?

When the quake happened, I was living in Honolulu, a good 3500 miles away, but within prime distance for the tsunami to wash up on our shores. For some context, the Hawaiian Islands has had two destructive tsunamis within the last century, both originating from sources well beyond our shores. There was nothing to suggest that this tsunami would be any different. We had about 6–7 hours to prepare for the inevitable. I remember getting all the emergency gear, food, water, shutting off all the electrics, etc, but above all, an overwhelming sense of fear among the people. The supermarkets, usually quite empty at that time of night, were filled with people getting emergency supplies. Every hour, the warning sirens would go off. In WWII, they were used to warn of attacking aircraft. Today, their presence is eerie, giving a sense of foreboding. It was almost a surreal feeling. It was around 3am when the first waves hit, just gentle ones lapping up the beach on Waikiki. Eventually though, the waves grew stronger in intensity. According to the government officials, the tallest one was about 7 feet. Smaller than expected, but big enough to cause millions of dollars in property damage. But due to the combined effects of good preparation and smaller than expected waves, no one would die. The same can’t be said for California, where a man tragically lost his life to the tsunami in Crescent City. When these kinds of things happen, there is not much else one can do other than to prepare yourself best for the inevitable. I remember going to the top of the high-rise condo I lived in. Being 48 stories high, I could only hope that it was sturdy enough to withstand the weight of the water. Many others took to the hills, causing huge traffic jams. Being stuck in a traffic jam during a tsunami is not ideal, hence why I didn’t follow that route. You can never really predict how bad things are going to get. You can only prepare yourself the best way possible and hope that your preparations were enough.

Question: What is the hottest planet in our Solar System? Is it the closest to the Sun?
Answer: The hottest planet in our Solar System is Venus. The second planet from the Sun, Venus is the hottest because of its incredibly thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, traps nearly all the heat that Venus receives from sunlight. Question: What are the differences between super-earths, mini-neptunes, and gas dwarfs?
Answer: A super earth is a rocky planet somewhere between 1–15 times the mass of Earth. Many Kepler planets discovered so far are super-earths. A super-Earth is usually discernible by its small radius (1–2 Earths) for its mass. Much like the Solar System’s terrestrial planets, super-Earths generally get denser the heavier they get while the radius stays the same. A mini-Neptune is in the same weight-class as a super-Earth, but instead of resembling the Earth and having a solid surface, a mini-Neptune would resemble Neptune, a gaseous composition. Gas dwarfs are the same as mini-Neptunes. Mini-neptunes in contrast to super-Earths are characterized by large radii for small masses, usually 3–5 Earth radii for an object weighing 5 Earth masses. The large radius and small mass indicates a gaseous composition, hence the moniker. It is unfortunate that we don’t have such a planet in our system, though imaginations can ponder what such a world may look like.

Question: What is the difference between 777-312 and 777-368 and other 777-300ERs?
Answer: The last two digits in the sequence represent what is known as the “Boeing customer code.” Each airline has a unique customer code to distinguish themselves from other airlines. Therefore, when they order a Boeing plane, the variant numbers will follow that sequence. An example is Cathay Pacific. Cathay Pacific has the Boeing 747–400, Boeing 777–200, 777–300, -300ER, and various freighter versions of the 747. Their Boeing customer code is -67. This means that any Boeing plane ordered by Cathay will have the variant number first followed by the customer code as the last two digits. For Cathay, this means that a Boeing 747–400 will be designated as 747–467, a 777–300ER as a 777–367ER, a 747–400ERF as 747–467ERF, and so on. Similarly, a 777–300ER ordered by Singapore Airlines will be designated as 777–312ER, and one ordered by All Nippon Airways as 777–381ER. There is no difference between any of these planes operating for different carriers other than the interior configurations and the fact that they are operated by different airlines and thus likely serve different mission profiles. The customer code is simply a way to distinguish one airline from another.

Question: What planet has the shortest rotation on its axis?
Answer: In our solar system, Jupiter takes the crown for fastest rotation. Although different parts of its atmosphere rotate at different speeds (the poles rotate slower than the equator), the consensus is that the period is around 9 hours 55 minutes. Outside our solar system however, there are a slew of planets with rotation rates so fast they would make Jupiter look like a slow-poke. Beta Pictoris b, a young giant planet orbiting the class A star Beta Pictoris, has a rotation rate of 8 hours. Because it still boasts a prematurely large radius due to its recent formation, theoretical models predict a planet of Beta Pictoris b’s class to rotate in as few as three hours once gravity is able to shrink the planet to its 0.8–1.0 Jupiter radii mature form. Faster still is the planet Kepler-39b. An 18 Jupiter mass planet orbiting its star in just 21 days, the radius of 1.25 Jupiters is too large for theoretical models which predict it to be at around 0.8–1.0 Jupiters given its age and temperature. Nevertheless, a recent discovery has shown that the planet is extremely oblate, so oblate that the estimated rotation rate is as little as 1.6 hours, some six times faster than Jupiter! The fast rotation also provides a natural explanation for the larger than normal radius. Finally, although not a planet, a notable mention is the brown dwarf WISEPC J112254.73+255021.5. If you thought Kepler-39b was fast, this brown dwarf completes one rotation anywhere between 17 to 51 minutes. So fast is the rotation rate of this Jupiter-sized object that radio flares are emitted from the object. Even though WISEPC J112254.73+255021.5. is not really a planet, it is still a cool prospect to imagine what life would be like with days being little over a half hour long. Forget eight-hour school days. You’d barely have enough time to eat breakfast in the morning before the new day came about. Whatever the case, it is a pretty cool object to study and ponder about.

Question: What is the Big Bang and when did it occur?
Answer: The Big Bang was the moment our Universe and everything in it came into existence. It occurred roughly 13.7 billion years ago according to data gathered from red-shifts of faraway galaxies caused by the ongoing expansion of the Universe. The Big Bang, although often thought of as an explosion, is actually more of an expansion. Many scientists agree that the term “Big Bang” is misleading. More appropriately, this event that marked the start of the Universe would be better labelled as “The Everywhere Expansion.” There is no one “centre” where the Universe started from. Rather, everywhere is expanding at the same time, much in the way a balloon expands when one inflates it. Whatever you choose to call it, the important point is that the Big Bang marks the start of our Universe as we know it.

Question: How does the transit method work in practice for exoplanet discovery?
Answer: The transit method detects an extrasolar planet when it passes in front of its star in relation to the Earth. Think of a transit as a mini-eclipse. When a planet transits the disk of its host star, the host star will dim slightly. The amount of dimming correlates directly to the radius of the planet. Transits can also help astronomers determine characteristics like atmospheric composition, temperature, and even the gravitational presence of additional bodies in the system not detected by the transits. While advantageous in many aspects, not every planet transits their star. For a transit to be observed from the viewpoint of the Earth, the planet’s orbit has to be oriented in a way that allows the orbit to cross the disk of the star based on the Earth’s vantage point. The technical terminology for this is “inclination.” Planets that transit their stars based on Earth’s vantage point are inclined around 90 degrees relative to the plane of the sky. Thus, many planets that aren’t inclined at 90 degrees will be missed by this method. The transit method also detects close-orbiting planets much easier, as a close-orbiting planet is more likely to transit than a far one. Nevertheless, the countless systems discovered by Kepler and the worlds of science we can apply to these newfound planets no doubt gives the transit method the credibility it needs

Question: How do scientists find planets at the distant stars if that star system is not planar from our point of observation, meaning the planets never cross their stars in front of us?
Answer: The most common way to find planets without a transit is the radial-velocity method. The radial velocity method takes the Doppler Spectroscopy of a star and watches how the light shifts from blue to red. As a planet orbits a star, its gravity will cause the star to wobble slightly, causing the star to move slightly further, then closer to the Earth. As the star moves along the planet’s orbit, its light spectrum gets shifted bluer as it moves closer, then redder as it moves further. By deducing the speed at which the star moves coupled with the total mass of the star, scientists can figure out the minimum mass and the orbital period of the planet, then deduce a total mass if the inclination is known. Many of the first known extrasolar planets such as 55 Cancri b, 51 Pegasi b, Tau Bootis b, and Upsilon Andromedae b were found using this method. Other methods, albeit less common, include gravitational microlensing, direct imaging, and pulsar timing. Gravitational microlensing plays on the idea of space-time being curved. If a foreground star moves between Earth and a more distant background star, the light of the background star will be warped by the dent the foreground star makes in space time. If a planet happens to orbit the foreground star, the warping caused by the foreground star will be altered slightly by the addtional well created by the planet’s dent in space-time. More commonly, this method is used to find black holes although it should be noted that several planets in the galactic bulge have been found this way. Direct imaging is exactly what it sounds like. Most commonly done through the infrared method, direct imaging has been used mainly to find gas giants several times the mass of Jupiter orbiting their bright host stars at relatively large separations. Most of the planets found using direct imaging are young because young gas giants have higher heat leftover from their formation, thus appearing more easily in the infrared spectrum. Finally, pulsar timing is used for pulsars. If a planet orbits a pulsar, it will cause the spin-rate of the pulsar to speed up or slow down, which will give the planet away since pulsars tend to spin at a constant pace. The first known planets orbiting the pulsar PSR 1257+12 were found this way. There are many methods to find planets not using he transit method. Planetary science is a growing school of knowledge and we can only look to the stars and our burgeoning technological advancements to thanks for our ever increasing understanding of these strange but awesome worlds.

Question: Is there any famous example of a caddy’s advice to a pro golfer leading directly to a tournament win?
Answer: On the 71st hole of the 1999 PGA Championship, Tiger Woods faced a seven-foot par-putt which could have altered the course of golfing history. Make it, and he’d have a one shot lead going into 18. Miss, and what little momentum he had left would have been sapped even less by the costly bogey. Despite his lead being as much as 5 shots at one-point in the day, a series of costly blunders combined with a charging Sergio Garcia made for a much more white knuckle situation. Caddie Stevie Williams was called in for the read. Tiger saw the putt outside left edge, but Stevie saw it inside the hole. Based on practice round knowledge, both of them knew the putt didn’t break as much as it looked. If played outside left edge, the putt may have never come back to the hole. Tiger decided to go ahead and trust the slightly differing read of inside left-edge given to him by his caddy, a huge mental hurdle for any golfer. The result? A clean-cut putt that found the center of the cup. Tiger would go on to par 18 and win by one, thanks to that par-save on the 17th green. If he’d not listened to Stevie Williams, the putt would have almost certainly missed, and Sergio’s first major may have come 18 years earlier. This tournament was a great example of how a good caddy can help a player in the most pressure-packed circumstances.

Question: What is it like to be a non-member attending a Mormon college or university?

Question: You are the Emperor of the Galactic Empire. How do you deal with the Rebels?
Answer: “Call up Mon Mothma and put me on the phone,” I said. She gulped, evidently taken aback. “Don’t look so surprised, you did just attack our base on Scarif not so long ago,” I said, referencing the debacle that was Orson Krennic’s failure. “I, um..” she stammered. “No matter, it was an impressive tactical victory. So much so that I am willing to offer a condition of peace to end this destructive conflict.” I waved Vader over. “And what may that be?” Mothma asked, the uneasiness in her voice evident?” “You will allow me to come to your base,” I said, waving my hand lazily. “I, umm…” her voice trailed off. “You will allow us to come to your base to negotiate peace talks,” Vader and I chanted, waving our hands at her. “Wow, I have a headache,” she gasped, the power of the mindtrick churning her brain. “You will allow us to come to your base to negotiate peace talks,” Vader and I chanted. “Fine. I will allow you to come to our base to negotiate peace talks, but no weapons,” she finally said. I smiled. “We do not need weapons in a moment of peace,” I said, gleaming. “Perfect. We will see you by the next rotation. Here are the coordinates,” she said, giving me the location of Yavin 4. Ah I thought, so that’s where they were hiding. “Tell Tarkin to ready the super-weapon, we are heading for Yavin IV. Forget the consort that escaped,” I told Vader. The next day: “Milord, we are approaching Yavin IV,” the bridge commander said. “Perfect,” I told him. I keyed the rebel frequency, calling up Mon Mothma. “Mon,” I breathed. “Emperor,” she said. “We have dropped out of hyperspace and are approaching, will be here in minutes. In the last minutes of our flight, we would like to acknowledge your existence as a soverign entity separate from the Galactic Empire. This destructive conflict has no place in our galaxy. Rather, I’d much prefer to hold diplomatic talks and peaceful resolutions to problems, wouldn’t you agree? “Why, yes, that does sound like an alternative to the fighting that’s been going on,” she said. I waved Vader over. “Unfortunately, with the recent events of Scarif, I have had no choice. I don’t want to do this, but you leave me no choice,” I said, sighing. I closed my eyes, reaching into the Force. A shatterpoint of energy concentrated on Mothma’s holo-signature, I was able to strangle it out of the Force, a butterfly crushed in the strength of my grip. When I opened my eyes, Mothma was on the floor, a pool of blood leaking from her agape mouth. Quickly, I waved Vader to the bridge before scurrying over myself. This would be a sight to enjoy. “Everybody, I’d like you to take a break from what you’re doing and witness the first full-powered test of this weapon, on the rebel base no less. We are now within firing range. Tarkin, please fire when ready,” I said. He nodded, a smirk on his face. “I do admit, this plan of yours was rather ingenius,” he admired. I beamed. “Your praise is most appreciated Governer,” I said. He smiled, then pulled the lever to unleash the full power of the battle station. The shuddering of the reactor core was followed by a green triangle which focused on a single point. Slowly, as the reactor spooled up, the shuddering intensified before giving way to a single loud explosion. A jet of plasma powered through the dark night, concentrating bolts of hell into the space Yavin IV once occupied. Rebel camp, wildlife, forests, and oceans all disintegrated in the moment of truth long awaited for. Through the Force, I could sense the cries of death from millions of beings. I paused to savor the moment of victory, hearing them be silenced abruptly as if a record player smashed by a hammer. “Incoming ship dropping out of hyperspace,” a radar operator said. “Use the surface guns and destroy them,” I said. Two shots marked the end of the Tantive IV and the rebels’ hopeless dreams of destabilizing the Empire. “We have done well men. Consider today a victory. Our peace talks were successful, from a certain point of view,” I mused, allowing the men to chortle. “Take the rest of the week off, and we will start afresh next week, mind you, without the terrorists who threaten to destabilize us. The galaxy is ours for good now. Well done,” I said, before stalking off to my cabin.

Question: If you were going to ignite a large gas giant so it became a small star, how would you do it?
Answer: I would add mass. A lot of mass. The reason the gas giant isn’t fusing is because it isn’t sufficiently massive to generate the kind of power needed to achieve runaway collapse to kick-start nuclear fusion. For the same reasons the Sun cannot fuse heavier elements than helium, the gas giant cannot fuse even hydrogen. As we all know, a star that cannot fuse hydrogen is no star, instead being either a brown dwarf or a large gas giant. Large gas giants and brown dwarfs can be somewhat blurred, so let’s assume you mean an object of 40 Jupiter masses as a large giant planet. The least massive star has a total mass of somewhere between 75–85 Jupiter masses, so if we use that star as a bench-mark, our hypothetical large gas-giant/brown-dwarf has to double its total mass to achieve that minimum bar to start nuclear fusion. For something like Jupiter? You’re gonna be spending a lot of time adding mass to that thing. To make a long story short, stars are big, and planets are not. There is a reason these things don’t fuse and shine like normal stars do.

Question: Why do airplanes only fly at 39000 feet and not higher?

Question: When an aircraft says to the tower that they are heavy, what does that mean?
Answer: The callsign “HEAVY” means that an aircraft is in a weight class above 300,000lbs. This generally refers to the gross MTOW, although a lightly-loaded aircraft in this weight class will use the HEAVY callsign even when not above the 300,000lb gross weight. The term HEAVY is more for wake turbulence, separation between aircraft due to the powerful vortexes generated by the passage of an aircraft through the same region of air. If an aircraft is too close to another, wake turbulence can disrupt the flight of an aircraft in unpleasant ways or in extreme cases, contribute to an accident. If an aircraft is a “HEAVY,” the controller can then take the necessary precautions to space other aircraft behind him accordingly.

Question: After a star goes supernova, a lot of matter is ejected into space. Why then is the resulting black hole the same mass as the original star?
Answer: It isn’t. The black hole is only the mass of the collapsed core that caused it to to supernova. If the resulting black hole is somewhere between 5–15 solar masses, the mass of the total star may have been as high as 60–100 solar masses at formation. Massive stars go through extreme mass loss in their twilight years. Stages such as the Wolf-Rayet or LBV can see stars losing more than 50 percent of their initial masses. As such, a 60–100 solar mass star may only be 15–20 solar masses by the time it goes supernova. Most of this stuff will end up in a nebula surrounding the star by the time it goes supernova. As the black hole comes from the core of the progenitor star, the resulting black hole ends up only a fraction of what the star once was in its younger years. Still, I wouldn’t advise messing with this thing.

Question: What are some facts about every planet?
Answer: Mercury: Orbits the Sun at an average distance of 0.38 AUs. Its radius is 0.38 Earths, while its surface gravity is also 0.38gs. Its mass is only 0.05 Earths while its orbit is the most eccentric of the eight major solar system planets at 0.206. As you all (hopefully) know, Mercury is also the closest planet to the Sun, orbiting the Sun in a short 88 days. This can raise the day temperature to a scorching 800 degrees Fahrenheit, 430 celsius, or 717 K roughly. But because Mercury’s atmosphere is essentially non-existent, it has no capacity to retain heat. The night-side is thus a bone-chilling -280 Fahrenheit, -170 celsius, or 83K. Surprisingly, Mercury also contains pockets of ice. Due to the extreme slow rotation (58 days) and the almost non-existent axial tilt, some places on the planet never see sunlight. These are the places water-ice can remain hidden, safe from the scorching sun. Mercury used to be geologically active, flood basalts and the like paving the surface for a brief period in its history. But owing to its size, Mercury became geologically dead long ago, due to the internal heat having been cooled sufficiently to no longer allow pockets of magma to reach the surface. Mercury also has an extremely long day, as I mentioned earlier. With a rotation rate of 58 days, an eccentricity of 0.2, and an orbital period of 88 days, such is the strangeness of this planet that the Sun actually moves backwards at a time during the orbit. Despite the rotation of the planet being 58 days, when the Sun is close to midday, the planet’s orbit at perihilion is actually faster than the planet’s rotation. This results in the Sun moving backwards in the sky, resulting in an even longer day. From sunrise to sunrise, you can expect to wait a toe-nail growing 176 days, or roughly two full orbits. Better pack some sunscreen and a sleeping bag. Venus: At first glance, Venus may appear to be similar to the Earth. Orbits the Sun at 0.72 AUs, orbital period of 225 days, mass of 0.81 Earths, radius of 0.95 Earth radii and a surface gravity of 0.903 g. Not a bad place at first glance. Even better, the equilibrium temperature is only 300K, or roughly the temperature of a hot summer day assuming a roughly Earth-like albedo. Who wouldn’t give to spend a couple days on a planet-wide tropical paradise where gravity is easier and flights are marginally shorter? But alas, Venus is far from a paradise, unless you live on Mustafar or some god-awful place like that. Venus is home to the densest atmosphere of all the terrestrial planets in the Solar System. It’s CO2 laden atmosphere traps so much heat that the temperature day or night is a whopping 860 Fahrenheit, 480 Celsius, or 760 Kelvin. To make matters worse, a full day here is actually longer than a year. If you could peek through the dense clouds of Venus, you’d have to wait a whopping 243 days from sunrise to sunrise. Talk about a long day. In the distant past, Venus may have started off with oceans like the Earth. Computer models are still trying to figure this out but it is possible. Anyhow, the Sun, despite being about 25 percent dimmer than today, was still two times brighter than it is today on Earth. Still, Venus may have resembled a hot desert planet like Tatooine. Harsh, but liveable if you farm enough moisture. But as all things go, the party only lasts for so long, and after a short period of 700 million to one billion years, the Sun heated up enough that the water likely evaporated. The runaway greenhouse kicked off, and voila, today we have a hell-house planet of CO2. Makes me wonder what we’re gonna do when that happens to us sooner or later, either through the Sun’s evolution or climate change gone awry. Anyways, back to Venus talk. Venus’s CO2 atmosphere is also one of the most reflective. It is the brightest object in the night sky from our vantage point. Such is its brightness that if you look closely, you can actually somewhat see phases of Venus much like phases of the Moon. I haven’t personally verified this, but from what I’ve seen, it’s pretty amazing. The geology of Venus is also somewhat difficult to study given the CO2 greenhouse and all, but we have made some improvements. Volcanoes run amok on Venus. The question is whether they are dead or alive. Much like Schrodinger’s cat problem, they could be dead, or alive. Previously, we thought they were dead, but recent evidence suggests that Maat Mons, the highest peak on Venus, may have evidence of recent geological activity. How fun! By the way, Maat Mons is 8km tall or 26,400 feet. He isn’t short by any means. Massive flood basalts also seem to have repaved the surface of this planet, the most recent being around 500 million years ago. Much like the Siberian Traps or the Deccan Plateau but on a larger scale, the magma probably oozed from every nook and cranny possible. It is possible that these major flooding events contribute to the CO2 in the atmosphere. If major volcanic events took place early in Venus’s history, they could have accelerated the loss of any surface water that may have existed. Earth: Also known as the Pale Blue Dot, the Blue Marble, humanity’s sandbox, etc, planet Earth is our home. Before I go on a philosophical tangent about our own home, let’s pause for a moment and just admire. Yup, that’s our home. Every dictator, monarch, natural disaster, celebrity, criminal, species, etc. have seen their entire histories written out on this beautiful blue marble. There are countless Earth-like planets out there. Many of them may have water. But this place is the only place we know of that harbors life, intelligent life at that. More a philosophical tangent than a scientific one, this planet is a treasure, our treasure. We must treat this place as if it were a gift from the cosmos, because it really is. Despite the trillions of planets out there, we still have no idea whether life was a biological accident or not. And even if it wasn’t, it’s still a hella long way to the next one. Cherish this gift my fellow Earthlings. You and your grandkids will thank yourselves for listening to me. Mars: Also known as the Red Planet, Mars is roughly 1/10th the mass of the Earth and around half the radius. Orbiting at 1.54 AUs, it takes 687 Earth days to take one trip around the Sun. A day on this planet is just 24 hrs and 40 mins. Mars is the home of many geological wonders. Olympus Mons, largest planetary mountain on Earth, is larger than the eight major Hawaiian Islands combined. At a height of 72,000 feet, it is more than twice the height of Mauna Kea, the Earth’s tallest planetary mountain at 33,800 feet from base to summit. The Valles Marineris is a canyon longer than the entire contiguous United States. Grand Canyon? That’s cute. This thing is 200km wide and more than 4,000km long. Mars also has two moons, Phobos and Deimos. These two are likely captured asteroids and more resemble potatoes than our own Moon. Mars is also the likely victim of a grand scheme by Jupiter and Saturn. Dubbed the “Grand Tack,” this theory basically says that the planet Jupiter, during its formation, migrated inward roughly to where the present day Mars is today. Because of Jupiter’s immense gravity, the proto-planetary disk where Mars was became relatively depleted, explaining for a relatively small mass. Current models of Solar System formation give Mars a much larger mass, somewhere between 1–2 Earth masses. This would make sense since the further you went from the Sun, the proto-planetary disk would become thicker with material. However, if you put a giant planet in the same region, the gravitational influence of the giant planet would excite the material too much to allow for any sort of sticking. The reason for a small Mars is explained quite well with the inward migration of Jupiter to 2.0 AUs, roughly 0.4 AUs away from the region where Mars currently orbits. Jupiter eventually receded to its present day location after the formation of Saturn. Mars on the other hand, was left stunted and too small. Had Mars been about the size of Earth or larger, perhaps it too could have supported a planetary ocean for longer. But the small mass made for a relatively weak magnetic field, allowing for solar radiation to strip away any substantial atmosphere the Red planet may have had. Today, the only pockets of water exist underground or near the polar ice caps and the atmospheric pressure is far too low to support liquid water. However, given a little terraforming, I could see Mars becoming more hospitable to us. Jupiter: We talked a bit about Jupiter earlier, but here we are again. Jupiter, the largest and most massive planet in the Solar System, is also the oldest and the kingpin of the eight major planets. Orbiting at 5.2 AUs, the gas giant takes 11.8 years to make one trip around the Sun. Jupiter is also the planet with the shortest day, taking just 9 hours and 56 minutes from sunrise to sunrise. Jupiter’s equilibrium temperature is quite low. Orbiting at 5.2 AUs, a perfect gray sphere would have a temperature of roughly -240 celsius. But Jupiter being so massive, it produces far more heat than it actually receives. If you were to reach a depth of say, 1000km, you’d already get temperatures far greater than anything you’d feel on Earth. Still, Jupiter’s distance from the Sun allows it to have clouds of ammonia, owing for its incredible brightness in the night sky. Storms also rage across this planet, the Great Red Spot being the most famous one. If you were to fit Earth into the Great Red Spot, you’d have room for another two planets. Despite its grandness today, Jupiter had relatively humble beginnings. Jupiter probably started off as a super-Earth type planet maybe 5–10 times the mass of Earth. Because the outer Solar system is cooler, ices and silicates were able to stick to the young proto-planet. The proto-planet was also massive enough to attract gas, predominantly hydrogen and helium. This growth started off rather slowly, taking perhaps 500,000–1 million years to reach 30 Earth masses. But once it reached a certain mass, the growth began to accelerate, taking less time to reach its current mass of 318 Earths than it did to reach 30 Earth masses. Jupiter was thus born. Being the first, it was able to scoop up the most material, leaving out other cores like Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and possibly others to scoop up the leftovers. We mentioned Jupiter’s Grand Tack migration, but what we didn’t was the likely planets Jupiter booted. The early Solar System was chaotic. Every early Solar System is chaotic. We know this from the countless hot Jupiters we’ve observed. Our Solar System was probably no different. Statistical modelling indicate that at least one, and possibly two, ice giants were formed and then ejected from the Solar System. The Late Heavy Bombardment, a period during which a rain of asteroids and comets crashed down upon the inner Solar System, may be explainable by one or two ice giant planets passing through the nascent Kuiper Belt. The statistical modelling actually suggests a likelier possibility of the current outer Solar System configuration happening if one or even two extra giant planets were booted by Jupiter. Anyhow, Jupiter is a big bully. We know that. But big bullies also look out for little guys, eventually anyways. Jupiter has 67 moons and counting, and a faint ring system. Being the largest, it is the most likely to capture and form the most. Some of Jupiter’s moons may not be larger than a refrigerator. But others may contain sub-surface oceans, volcanoes, and possibly life. Jupiter’s moons are a world of their own, and there is not nearly enough space to write about all of them. Jupiter is also massive enough to outweigh all the other planets combined and still have enough room to spare. Jupiter, at 318 Earth masses, is 2.5 times heavier than the rest of the planets, asteroids, comets, and loose junk in our Solar System. Such is Jupiter’s mass that it is sometimes erronously referred to as a failed star. I went over this in another answer, but I’ll go over it again. Jupiter is not a failed star. It is an intermediate-mass gas giant planet, a fairly common planetary type in the galaxy. However, Jupiter’s mass and radius are large enough to be used as a unit of measurement, and is often done so in the world of exoplanetology. Extrasolar gas giants and brown dwarfs are often measured in “Jupiter masses and Jupiter radii.” If a gas-giant 5-times heavier was observed around another star, it would be referred to as a “5-Jupiter mass planet.” If its radius was then determined to be 0.9 Jupiters, it may be referred to as a “0.9 Jupiter radii planet.” Judging based on Jupiter’s mass and size, we can understand the compositions and ages of other planets based on their masses and sizes. A giant planet with 5-Jupiter masses and 0.9 radii may be composed of the same material as Jupiter and be roughly the same age, while the same planet but with a 1.5 Jupiter radius would be recognized as being younger or hotter. Much as we use kilograms and kilometers, Jupiter’s dimensions can be used as a “kilometer” or “kilogram” in astronomy. Saturn: Home to the largest ring system in our Solar System, Saturn may be affectionally dubbed as the “Ring Planet.” At 0.3 Jupiter masses but 0.8 times the radius, Saturn is actually light enough to float on water, if you could get a big enough bathtub. Saturn is also the most oblate planet, due to its speedy rotation of 10 hrs 42 minutes. Orbiting at 9.5 AUs, Saturn takes a good 29.5 years to go around the Sun once. Average temperatures range from -150 to -200 celsius, but due to internal heat, the atmosphere is a lot warmer the deeper you go. Much like Jupiter, it radiates far more heat than it receives. Still, its distance from the Sun allows it ammonia clouds, giving it the brightness that allows us to view it from such a great distance. Saturn is also quite unique, being the only planet to boast a substantial ring system. Current models of giant planet formation give all four planets huge rings in the beginning. Satellites like the Galilean Moons or Titan form out of these disks. But eventually, due to satellites carving material out, these disks disappear, leaving very faint remnants detectable only through close scrutiny. Saturn however, still wears its rings loud and proud. First observed by Galileo, they are probably remnants of one or more moons pulled apart by Saturn’s gravitational pull. It is unclear how long they have been here, but theories range from the rings being a temporary sideshow to a permanent decoration present since the birth of the Solar System. I won’t be the one to tell you which theory to listen to, so we’ll just leave it at that. Saturn’s moons are also quite extensive, almost being as plentiful as Jupiter. One of them, Titan, is the only satellite boasting a substantial atmosphere in the entire Solar System. While other satellites do have atmospheres, Titan’s atmosphere is enough to support liquid methane on its surface. While methane is gross to us humans, it may actually be friendly to other forms of life. Who knows? Maybe Titan’s methane lakes contain some sort of bacteria we’ve never before heard of. Another one of Saturn’s moons, Enceladus, is home to a huge underwater ocean. Hydrothermal vents make for the possibility of deep sea life through a heat source. Plumes of water vapour have been observed on this moon as well, leading further precedent to the heated vents theory. Despite its large distance from the Sun, Saturn’s moons may be some of the best candidates for extraterrestrial life in our Solar System. Who knows? Maybe one day we’ll find out. Uranus: This planet is an oddball. Just everything about it is strange. For starters, it orbits an incredible 18.18 AUs from the Sun. You have no idea how far this is. As far away as Saturn is from the Sun, Uranus is nearly double that distance. One trip around the Sun takes 84 years. But get this. Uranus, unlike the other planets, is tilted a good 90 degrees. Yup, you got it. Uranus is a giant bowling ball rolling along. Current theory suggests that a super-Earth smashed into Uranus long ago, knocking it onto its side. This gives some areas, specifically the poor poles, a long half-year in sunlight, and a long half-year in darkness. Did I mention a half-year here is 42 years? Heck, I’d go crazy spending almost half a century in darkness and another almost half in sunlight. Uranus is also cold, very cold. Unlike Jupiter and Saturn, Uranus emits roughly the same amount of energy it receives from the Sun. The giant impact from above may or may not explain the relative lack of internal heat. This makes Uranus the coldest planet in the Solar System. At -356 F, -216 C, or 57K, the cloud tops of this planet are colder than liquid nitrogen. Uranus’s surface gravity is also lower than that of the Earth, despite being 14 times heavier. This is owing to the fact of a large radius. At 4 Earth radii, Uranus is the third largest planet in the Solar System and the second least-dense, though not as much so as Saturn. Uranus’s moons are also the smallest in the Solar System of the four giant planets. Unlike Jupiter and Saturn, Uranus lacks a large satellite for company. Even so, Uranus is home to 27 moons and a small but visible ring system. The largest moon, Titania, is roughly 60 percent the radius of Pluto. Uranus’s moons and rings also orbit following its axial tilt, suggesting that whatever formed may have done so after the collision. The collision may also explain the lack of large satellites around Uranus, as the impact and residual from the collision may have destroyed anything forming at the time. Uranus is visible with the naked eye. However, at a magnitude of +5.5 and a distance of over 2 billion km, any discernable movement is almost unnoticeable. For this very reason, Uranus was not recognized as a major planet until 1781, when William Herschel happened to recognize what he was looking at. Hipparchos, almost two millennia earlier, is possibly the first person to see Uranus, but owing to its extreme distance, did not recognize what he was seeing. Uranus became the first planet to be discovered through a telescope. Neptune: The furthest of the eight major planets, Neptune was the first planet discovered by inference through the position of another known planet. First observed in 1613 by Galileo, it like Uranus was not recognized as a planet until 1846, when peculiarities in Uranus’s orbit were found. Nearly two times times further from the Sun than Uranus, Neptune takes a good 164.8 years to orbit the Sun. Orbiting at 30.1 AUs, it is nearly 3 billion miles from the Sun on average. Despite this incredible distance, Neptune is home to the strongest winds in the Solar System. If you were to simply stand still, you’d achieve supersonic speeds. Neptune’s winds howl at an incredible 1,500mph, almost three times faster than a Boeing 767 at 33,000 feet. At 18 Earth-masses, Neptune is more massive but slightly smaller than its counterpart Uranus, but the two may as well be night and day in terms of internal heat. Neptune radiates far more heat than it receives, following the trend established by Jupiter and Saturn. Also being the furthest of the eight major planets, Neptune has the largest Hill Sphere or field of gravitational influence. One major moon, Triton, is a likely captured Kuiper Belt object, orbiting the planet in retrograde. Its orbit decaying, Triton will likely be destroyed sometime in the next 4 billion years, during which a Saturn-like ring system will be created. Neptune is home to 13 moons besides Triton and counting. Much like Uranus however, these other moons are irregular and tiny compared to the Galilean moons or Titan. This stems from the likely catastrophic impact of Neptune capturing Triton. Neptune’s original satellites, likely more massive than the current bunch, were probably destroyed or ejected during close encounters with Triton. A faint ring system is all that remains of this first generation of satellites. Neptune and Uranus are also hosts of diamond rain, exotic forms of precipitation only possible under the higher pressures of gas giant atmospheres. Along with Jupiter and Saturn, the two ice giants make for a fitting bookend to our tour of the major Solar System planets. Pluto Thought we were done? Think again. Remember, not so long ago, we had nine planets until one of them was famously demoted for being too small to clear its orbit. Enter Pluto No, not him! There we go. Excuse my humor. Pluto, the first Kuiper Belt object to be discovered, was originally thought to be a planet when peculiarities in Neptune’s orbit were thought to be caused by another major planet. Since Neptune was discovered in much the same way, astronomers turned their eyes to the skies again in search for this new ninth planet. In 1930, Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto, a discovery long thought to be the ninth planet of the Solar System. But alas, Pluto was extremely faint for how big they thought it was. Originally, they thought Pluto would have been in the Super-Earth category, although back then, such a term didn’t exist. Anyhow, as Pluto was so faint, they thought that the surface must be extremely dark, thus not reflecting a lot of light that hit the surface. But as telescope imagery got better, it quickly became revealed that far from dark, Pluto was actually extremely bright, just incredibly small. Over time, astronomers realized that Pluto wasn’t the planet they were looking for, and that the peculiarities in Neptune’s orbit were in fact errors. Anyhow, as Pluto had been discovered anyways, it became known as our ninth planet and stayed that way until the discovery of Eris, Sedna, and a bunch of other Kuiper Belt Objects. Quickly, it became realized that rather than a planet, Pluto was instead a member of a large ring of objects at the edge of the Solar System totaling perhaps in the thousands. As such, in 2006, the IAU held a meeting whether to recognize all these objects as planets, or to demote Pluto to “dwarf planet.” As recognizing all these other objects would prove complicated, we decided to change Pluto to a dwarf planet, making it one of the largest members of a new sub-class of substellar body. Still, just because Pluto is a dwarf planet does not mean it lacks substance. Pluto is host to five moons, more than any of the terrestrial planets. In fact, Pluto’s largest moon, Charon, is the largest satellite in the Solar System both by mass and radius when compared to its parent. Pluto also has blue skies, a fact verified by the fly-by of New Horizons in 2015. Isn’t that wonderful? Alas, at a distance of 39.5 AUs, it is also extremely dark and cold, temperatures dipping into the 30–40 Kelvin range. Solid nitrogen and methane exists on the surface. But cold does not mean dull. Pluto may actually be geologically active. Although at a great distance, it is still quite hard to tell. But when New Horizons flew by, traces of geological activity were found. The surface was surprisingly quite young, evidence of major geological resurfacing in astronomically recent timescales. Below is a beautiful picture of the surface of Pluto, taken from New Horizons during its fly-by. Note how smooth the surface seems to be in some parts. Rather than pock-marked like Mercury or the Moon, Pluto more closely resembles Mars or Titan. Perhaps some form of liquid (likely nitrogen) serves to shape the surrounding surface. In any case, this tiny dwarf planet is a lot more fascinating than one would imagine so. Planets beyond Neptune: Shortly after the discovery of Neptune, scientists soon turned to look for a ninth planet, based on peculiarities in its orbit. Although these peculiarities later turned out to be spurious, the discovery of Pluto among others got people wondering if there was anything else we didn’t know about. For a long time, it was assumed that beyond Pluto, there was nothing. But eventually, things like the Oort Cloud, Kuiper Belt, etc. were proposed and confirmed. Still, it seemed hard to see evidence of anything beyond Neptune, since if it were there, we would have found it already. However, in 2003, astronomers discovered an object called Sedna, a dwarf planet resembling Pluto but orbiting much farther away from the Sun and in a much more elliptical orbit. During its closest approach to the Sun, Sedna is already roughly 80 AUs away, or more than twice that of Pluto’s average distance. But at its furthest, Sedna is nearly 1000 AUs away, an orbit taking it toward the lower limit of the inner Oort Cloud. The discovery of such an object surprised astronomers so much that eventually, people started wondering if there really was a Planet 9 out there. Enter Mike Brown, Pluto-killer and his partner, reknown planetary astronomer Konstantin Batygin. In 2016, they mapped the orbits of Sedna and six other Kuiper Belt objects with similar orbits. Through careful statistical analysis and computer simulations, they found that these six objects along with Sedna were aligned in roughly the same direction, making them coplanar. Owing to their huge orbits and eccentricities, the chances of this being a coincidence are less than 0.007 of a percent, or less than one in one thousand. The favored explanation was a super-Earth or ice-giant somewhere between 5-10 times the mass of the Earth in an eccentric orbit ranging from 200AUs at perihelion to 2000 AUs at aphelion. If it exists, this planet would bridge the gap between terrestrial planets like Earth and ice giants like Uranus or Neptune. If it exists, it could provide meaningful information on the history of the Solar System and why some systems look so completely different than us. Other issues like slight tilting of the eight known planet’s orbits can also be explained by the existence of the new proposed planet. Epilogue Each planet is unique in its own way, but my favorite planet out of all of them is Earth. Despite the exotic diamond rain on Neptune, the huge canyons of Mars, underwater oceans of Europa, at the end of the day, I’d rather return to the Pale Blue Dot I know as home. Our corner of the Universe, no place will be dearer to my heart than the most beautiful blue jewel in the galaxy.

Name: Andrew Chin
Question: Which is the biggest, brightest, and hottest star in the universe that we humans know of?
Answer: Largest: UY Scuti, but it’s debatable There are several contenders, all of which I will name. Brightest: R136a1 By brightest, I am assuming you mean most luminous. R136a1 at 8.7 million solar luminosities is the most luminous hands down. A 315 solar mass WNh7 star, it will continue to brighten in the years to come as it continues to evolve. Hottest: WR 142 Now, this is the most complicated part of the question. By hottest, I assume you mean surface temperature. White dwarfs and stellar remnants aside, the hottest stars by surface temperature would be oxygen-sequence Wolf-Rayet stars, specifically the WOx type. A WOx wolf-rayet star is a Wolf-Rayet star whose atmosphere is dominated by oxygen. Most Wolf-Rayet star spectrums are dominated by hydrogen, helium, and carbon, thus being classified as WNxh, WNx, or WCx in that order. But oxygen-sequence stars, exceedingly rare due to their astronomically short-life-spans, receive the WOx designation. In our entire galaxy, only four are known, one of which is a contender for hottest star. Meet WR 142. Despite having nearly 20 times the mass of the Sun, its radius is only 0.4 solar radii, one of the reasons this thing is so hot. As a general law of thermodynamics, contracting gas heats up, and for the same reason red supergiant surfaces are large and cool, this one is extremely hot and small. With a surface temperature of 200,000K, this star is 4 times hotter than a typical O-type star, and is so hot most light is emitted in the UV spectrum. Despite being only 0.4 solar radii, the star is a good 500,000 times brighter, although visually, it is only 847 times brighter. Again, most light is in the UV spectrum due to the extremely hot stellar surface, further necessitating the use of sunscreen for any poor souls stuck in orbit around this terrible place. Who called Tatooine? So there you have it. I don’t know about you, but I prefer our own Sun to any of these other monsters on this list. Call me boring or lame, but I prefer a star that won’t fry me to a UV-laden crisp or worse, straight-up try to eat me when I decide to go to the beach. Now isn’t that nice?

Name: Andrew Chin
Question: Is it possible that one star is larger than the earth?
Answer: Of course it is. Every star sans stellar remnants is larger than the Earth. A star has to be at least 80 times the mass of Jupiter to ignite fusion, and something that huge crammed into a space the size of Earth simply wouldn’t work. Stars are much bigger than planets. Compared to stars, the Earth is like a speck of dust, a pale blue dot in the vast expanse of space. This photo of the pale blue dot illustrates exactly how small we are. Space is big people, accept it.

Name: Andrew Chin
Question: What is the brightest star in the Universe?
Answer: We don’t know exactly, but one star in the LMC comes pretty close to the theoretical limits. Meet R136a1. At 315 solar masses, it is nearly double the mass of interstellar titans like Eta Carinae, the Pistol Star, the Peony Star, among others. At 8.7 million solar luminosities, an Earth-like planet would have to orbit at an astounding 3,000 AUs, roughly the distance to the inner Oort Cloud. If it was in the place of the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, R136a1 would be as bright as the full moon and easily visible in the daytime. Such is the ferocity of this star that it emits as much radiation in five seconds as the Sun in an entire year. R136a1 is young, only one million years old, but it is already a middle-aged star for its mass. Already a WNh Wolf-Rayet star, it will eventually transition to become hydrogen free, and lose nearly all of its mass before detonating in a huge supernova. Total lifespan? 2 million years more or less. For comparison, at 2 million years, the Earth wasn’t even born yet! R136a1 lives fast but will die young. Despite the grandness that may come by living around a star like that, I much prefer our quiet and relatively peaceful G2V dwarf.

Name: Andrew Chin
Question: What are some strange but awesome exoplanets?
Answer: COROT-7b. Orbiting roughly 60 times closer to its star than Earth, this planet is a literal interpretation of hell. With surface temperatures ranging from 2,300K-3,100K, not even rock can remain as a solid. Oceans of lava bathe the day-side of this planet in a volcanic hell not unlike what Mustafar may look like. One year on this planet is as short as 20 hours. Imagine that. If you were able to survive the heat and enjoy a drink at the foot of the planet-wide ocean of lava, you’d be able to celebrate a birthday every 20 hours. Speaking of days, because the planet is so close to the star, one side is permanently locked in the blast furnace of the star while the other is plunged into the black of eternal night. The temperature difference between night and day may be as much as 2000Ks. Where oceans of lava may bathe the day, the nightside may much resemble the night-side of Mercury, with pockets of ice hidden deep in the safety of night. Alternatively, if the tidal pull from the star is enough (it probably is) the night side may be covered in volcanic hell as well. Jupiter’s moon Io comes to mind. Not exactly the lame H20 oceans we enjoy on Earth. What little atmosphere exists on this planet consists of wisps of vaporized clouds of iron, silicon, titanium, magnesium, potassium, etc. These elements condense to form a very alien and unpleasant form of 2,000 degree rain, however that may look like. The heat difference from day and night probably combines to make a pretty powerful jetstream, but the atmosphere being so thin, it probably wouldn’t feel all that much. Still, I can imagine hurricanes of molten iron forming over the twilight zones of this planet. What a world this place is. 2MASS J119–1137 AB If you thought COROT-7b was weird, wait till you meet the binary system of 2MASS J1119–1137 AB. Where COROT-7b was nice and snug to its home star, this couplet of 4-Jupiter mass planets wanders aimlessly through space starless, but with each other for company. You see, it turns out they actually orbit each other at a distance roughly comparable to the asteroid belt. While not technically moons to each other, I’d say these two qualify as the first bona-fide binary planet discovered. Their planet-like mass of 4 Jupiter masses strengthens the case for them to be bona-fide binary planets. After all, we’ve detected hundreds of planets heavier than these two, and whether or not they orbit stars or how they formed, they still deserve a mention in this post. NGC 4349–127 b Few exoplanets have been found orbiting high-mass stars, but planet NGC 4349–127 b is exactly one of those few planets. The star, currently a class M bright giant at 3.9 solar masses, was easily somewhere between 5–6 solar masses when accounting for high-mass loss rates associated with evolved stars in this mass range. When on the main-sequence, the star was likely of class B, probably somewhere between B4-B6. This would put it slightly brighter and more massive than the stars comprising the Pleiades’ famous Seven Sisters, pictured below. Imagine being on a planet orbiting a star of such grandness. Today, as a bright giant, NGC 4349–127 emits between 4,500–5,000 times more light than the Sun. The planet, a 19-Jupiter mass gas giant, orbits slightly beyond where Mars would be in the solar system at roughly 2.38 AUs. Despite this relatively far distance, it receives around 1,000 times the amount of light the Earth does. The equivalent temperature would likely be high, probably over 1500K. Any moons orbiting this planet would be covered in lava. If an Earth-like planet were to orbit this star, it would have to be near 70 times farther than the Earth is to the Sun, or roughly in the middle of the Kuiper Belt. Eventually, when this star reaches the tip of the AGB, it will likely be north of 20,000 times brighter than the Sun and perhaps 600 times the size. Orbiting at just 2.38 AUs, there is a more than even chance the planet will be engulfed by the expanding star before it goes out. HD 20782 b If you thought any of the above planets were strange, wait till you meet this one. This planet is a 1.8 Jupiter mass gas giant whose average distance from the Sun is around 1.4 AUs, or slightly less than Mars. Not extreme in the sense of other planets we have seen so far. But what’s crazy about this planet is the extreme eccentricity. At an eccentricity of 0.97, this planet has the highest known eccentricity of any planet we have found so far, and is unlikely to be exceeded by much. To see how extreme this orbit really is, Halley’s comet has an eccentricity of 0.96, or slightly less than this thing, which is a super-Jupiter by the way. Imagine if our own Jupiter was this badly behaved? If in our Solar System, its crazy orbit would range from 3 times closer to the Sun than Mercury to 3 times farther than Earth in the winter. Temperatures would range from below -150 celsius in winter to north of 1,500 celsius in summer. A moon of this planet would see its surface melted molten in the summer, frozen in a freeze worse than the deepest of Antarctica, and relatively Earth-like in the spring and the fall. Inhabitants of a moon here would really cherish the term “spring break.” I can’t even imagine what the weather would be like. For those looking to get four full seasons, here is your dream paradise. KELT-9b Two planets above, we met NGC 4349–127b, which orbits a former B-class star at a relatively toasty distance of 2.38 AUs. Question: As we are constantly finding similar planet types in exo systems, is it possible that a planet’s chemical constituents depend on its distance from the local star, star type, and size?
Answer: Depending on where it forms, yes. As we now know, planets tend to migrate, sometimes large distances from where they form. We see gas giants up close to their stars, super-Earth planets in extremely packed systems, isolated worlds in deep space, etc. Where a planet is and where it formed may not be the same thing, but both are important to determining its chemical composition and atmospheric makeup. A great example would be the planet Jupiter. Jupiter, having formed in the outer Solar system, has significant amounts of water-ice, silicates, rock, gas, etc. This is a product of it having formed beyond the snow-line, a region in the solar system where ices can stick together. As Jupiter is still beyond this ice line, it’s weather patterns and atmospheric content is largely reflective of it being in the colder regions of the Solar System. But if you were to move Jupiter closer to the Sun, say, to where Mercury is, some of the elements in Jupiter’s atmosphere may have a hard time staying in their present forms, allowing heavier elements that thrive at higher temperatures to come out. The current Jupiter has ammonia crystals and a large large amount of hydrogen and helium. However, if Jupiter was where Mercury was, it may be too hot for some of those elements. A Jupiter at Mercury’s orbit may instead have a cloudless atmosphere, combined with Rayleigh scattering that would turn the planet blue. If you moved it even closer to the Sun, say, to 1/10th of where Mercury is, you may get clouds of Titanium-oxide, iron, silicates to appear in the upper atmosphere. The hydrogen, helium, water-ice, etc would likely boil off in a tail behind the planet. We know of several evaporating gas giants that share this unfortunate fate. Now, a Jupiter that formed at Mercury’s orbit would be much different too. A Jupiter that forms at Mercury’s orbit may contain a lot of heavier elements, since the lighter elements like hydrogen and helium may find a hard time sticking together. Such planets may be rich in carbon and oxygen. Such a planet would be made up completely different from the gas giants in our Solar System, despite sharing the same mass. Star type matters too, since each star type is hotter or cooler depending on where on the HR diagram you went. If you formed a giant planet at 5 AU around a G-star, it would look much like Jupiter. Form it around a B or an O-star and it may look much like a gas giant that formed in the inner regions of a system. Talking about massive stars, it is likely that these massive stars have a higher chance of forming heavier and bigger planets, simply because their planet-forming material may be greater. Alas, we do find high-mass gas giants around lower-mass stars, but planets around A, B, or O stars would tend to be on the higher end of the mass scale. Most of the data we have obtained so far seems to support this, although it may just be a sampling bias that produces this effect. Stellar metallicity has a big factor too. Stars which have poor metallicity may form predominantly gas or hydrogen-rich planets while stars with high metallicity may end up having rocky planets 10 or more times heavier than the Earth. Everything that could affect a planet will, either it’s make-up, size, atmosphere, appearance, etc. As with snowflakes, no two systems are the same, and each planet is its own unique individual.

Question: Colors of stars are determined by temperature. Does that mean each star has a unique spectrum?
Answer: Yes they do. Each star has a unique spectral classification which can be used to tell a lot more about it. For example, the Sun is a G2V class star. This means that the Sun is of class G, is towards the brighter side of the G-class stars, and is a main-sequence star. The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram is quite useful in determining where a star is in terms of spectrum. As you can see here, the plot of main-sequence stars falls in a roughly linear trend from top left to bottom right. The hottest and most massive stars would be of class O, all the way on the top left, while the coolest and smallest stars would be of class M, all the way toward the bottom right. Our Sun as a class G star would be somewhere in the middle. All the stars on the main-sequence would be class V stars, meaning they are on the main-sequence. If you look toward the top right, you will see the stars that have evolved off the main-sequence. These stars are cooler and larger than their main-sequence counterparts, and are also much brighter. Evolved star classifications range all the way from IV for subgiants to class 0/Ia+ for the brightest and most luminous supergiant stars. An example of a well-known evolved star is Betelgeuse. Betelgeuse, a roughly 12 solar-mass star, was likely of class O when it was on the main-sequence. Today however, it is a class M1Ia-ab star. M1 means it is of class M, on the far right of the HR diagram. Ia-ab means it is on the cusp between a luminous supergiant and an intermediate-luminous supergiant. This would place it roughly 1–2 classes below the most luminous M-class supergiants like Mu Cephei and VY Canis Majoris. On the deep bottom left are where the white dwarves and stellar remnants exist. Because white dwarfs usually have surface temperatures in the 30–100,000K range, they are on the left, but as they are extremely dim, they are also on the bottom of the whole plot. These stars would receive a classification of D or C. As you can see, spectral classification is a unique way to determine the characteristics of a star. With the star having its own spectral footprint, it is hard to get bored with classifying different objects.

Question: How come the further a planet is away from a star, the colder it becomes?
Answer: The anount of radiation an object receives from a star decreases by the inverse square of the distance it is at. For example, a planet 2 times more distant than the Earth will receive 4 times less total radiation than the Earth does, while an object 3 times closer (Mercury) would receive approximately 9 times the amount of radiation. This means that the further a planet is from a star, the amount of light energy is decreased proportionally. By this same token, the planetary equilibrium temperature of an object would decrease accordingly. The planetary equilibrium temperature is basically what the temperature of the planet would be given amount of starlight and without the effects of atmospheres or albedo. Planetary equilibrium temperature - Wikipedia Of course, given that most planets have atmospheres, the actual temperature of planets can be sometimes very different from the planetary equilibrium temperature. Venus, as an example, has an equilibrium temperature of roughly 227K, but has an actual temperature of nearly 800K! But given the amount of starlight received, it should theoretically have a temperature similar to that of Earth. But oddballs aside, the inverse square law of electromagnetic radiation coupled with the planetary equilibrium should be sufficient in determining roughly how hot a planet should be, minus the effects of a greenhouse.
