Question: What planet in the universe has the highest known orbital eccentricity?
Answer: Meet planet HD 20782 b. With an orbital eccentricity of 0.97, this planet has an eccentricity slightly greater than that of Halley’s comet. If in our Solar System, its crazy orbit would bring it out beyond the asteroid belt, then a sizzling three times closer to the Sun than Mercury. The Extrasolar Planet Encyclopaedia Above is a pretty little picture of what the planet’s orbit looks like. If you thought our seasons were extreme, imagine what living on a moon of this planet would be like? You’d go from the literal deep-freeze of Hoth, all the way to temperatures hotter than molten lava, and back again. All within one calendar year. Earth’s lowest and highest temperature records stand a paltry 146K apart. On this world? These records may be more than 1200K different. I can’t even imagine what the weather patterns on this world would look like. If you’re like me and everybody else, you’re probably wondering how this poor planet ended up like this. While nobody knows for sure, one of the more popular theories involves the Kozai mechanism. The Kozai mechanism involves a secondary object, either a binary star or a more massive planet or brown dwarf orbiting further out than the eccentric planet or third body. Basically, the TLDR version of this involves the secondary star working to gradually tilt the orbit of the planet/third-body by constant gravitational pertubations over a large period of time. Eventually, the accumulated inputs by the other object would increase the eccentricity of the planet. Kozai mechanism - Wikipedia. In the case of HD 20782, the Kozai mechanism actually lends itself quite well because a secondary star, HD 20781, is present. HD 20781 - Wikipedia At roughly 0.76 Solar masses and orbiting about 9000 AUs away, it definitely has enough mass and is close enough to slowly increase the eccentricity of the planet. Coincidentally, this secondary star also has planets, but for this question, those are irrelevant. Several of my friends who are astronomers prefer this Kozai mechanism as the favored method to explain this planet, but again as I stress, these are only theories. The other theory I hear discussed a lot involves planet-planet scattering, but the problem with proving this theory is the lack of the other planet that would have caused such a large disruption in the orbit of this planet. That’s not to say that it couldn’t have happened, but with the lack of the other planet (likely ejected or destroyed), it will be hard to prove. Still, when computer simulations and statistical modeling gets better, we may be pleasantly surprised. No matter what caused it, the fact is that the planet is there, and it is up to us to figure out what happened to it. This, I suppose, is the beauty of science, to discover, to learn, and to explore.

Question: What's the largest known planet?
Answer: The largest known planet so far is HD 100546 b. At 6.9 Jupiter radii, it dwarfs everything else that we currently know of. HD 100546 - Wikipedia The reason it is so big is that it is extremely young for a planet, less than 10 Mya. Question: When the sun becomes a red giant, will Pluto, Titan and Enceladus become habitable?
Answer: Yes they will. A star like the Sun will go through two main red-giant phases, one when it runs out of hydrogen, and another when it runs out of helium. The first stage, called the red-giant branch, occurs toward the end of the subgiant phase, and for a star like the Sun, would happen somewhere around 12 Gyr after formation. To put a timeframe on this, we are currently at 4.6 Gyr, so still about 7 Gyrs away from this phase. A star like the Sun will spend about 0.5 Gyr on the red giant branch, gradually swelling and brightening until it reaches a size of 250 times present-day and 2–3,000 times brighter than today. To figure out the habitable zone of the Sun at the tip of the red-giant branch, we take the square-root of the estimated luminosity of the star in units of present day solar luminosities. The product will appear units of AUs, or in other words, Earth-Sun distances. For rounding purposes, we will use a figure of 2,500 solar luminosities for the Sun at the tip of the RGB. The square root of 2,500 gives us a figure of 50 astronomical units, so slightly beyond the distance where Pluto currently orbits. Obviously, this is not where the Sun will be in terms of constant brightness. In fact, it will have been brightening steadily over the course of about 500 million years. All the outer planets will see a drastic change in terms of sunlight radiation and heat. Jupiter, at the toasty distance of 5.2 AUs, would receive Earth-like radiation for a relatively short time, but eventually will receive more sunlight than even Mercury does today. Much like the hot Jupiters seen in other solar systems, it will be appropriately labelled a “roaster” planet, with surface temperatures ranging between 700–1200K. It’s safe to say there is not much prospect for life around any moons here. Even taking into account the mass loss from the increased stellar wind, Jupiter’s orbit would still be well below any habitable zone the red giant Sun would have. But Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune will be at relatively safer distances. Saturn, at 9.5 AUs, would receive Earth-like amounts of sunlight for much longer. While Jupiter roasts in a hellish environment, the heat would be just right for Saturn for much longer. Keep in mind that habitable zones for evolved stars are much wider than for their counterparts on the main sequence. A region as large as 20–30 AUs across may be habitable to any planets that may reside within. Of course, it is hard to tell when and for how long Saturn would be in the habitable zone, but let’s just say it would be a lot longer than Jupiter would be. Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and even Pluto may be habitable at the same time, depending on how the orbits of each planet evolved based on the mass loss of the Sun. This is where the moons of Titan and Enceladus come in. If their respective parent planet resides in the habitable zone, then it is very likely that the moons themselves would become oceans upon oceans. The only possible caveat would be the lack of atmospheric pressure. Objects of lighter mass tend to lose much of their atmospheres at Earth-like or greater temperatures, Mars and the Moon being several examples. While the heating of the worlds would give a thawing effect much like we’d see on a frozen meat pie, the relatively light mass of the moons would give them a lesser chance of being able to hold a substantial enough atmosphere to allow water to flow freely. Without an atmosphere, a planetary body would become much like the Moon, an airless world devoid of any chance of life. Enceladus, being the least massive and the closest to the Sun, would be the most likely to lose its water due to lack of atmospheric pressure. But Titan, already having a substantial atmosphere and much more mass, would stand a much better chance. Resembling a younger version of Earth, it may very well turn out to be the sweet spot of the Solar System. While lighter gases like hydrogen and helium will no doubt escape, Titan would be unlikely to lose all of its atmosphere, especially the heavier gases like nitrogen and oxygen. With appropriate atmospheric pressure and the heat from the evolved Sun, it may indeed resemble a warmer and wetter version of Mars. During the RGB, Titan may have about 200 million years of habitability. Only toward the end of the RGB will Titan receive unsafe levels of radiation, during which we may have to escape all the way to Pluto. Speaking of Pluto, the sunlight received on Pluto would be comparable to that of a typical Martian day for much of the RGB, but towards the end, the solar radiation would become comparable to that of Earth. Atmospheric gases are unlikely to escape except toward the end, but in any case, we wouldn’t have to stay there for that long. I mentioned earlier that this phase was only temporary. Toward the end of the RGB, the Sun will run out of hydrogen. This will result in the core collapsing to fuse helium, resulting in a helium flash event. During this helium flash, the Sun will brighten momentarily, then shrink to a size perhaps about 10 times its current radius, with the luminosity being somewhere between 50 times that of today. Again, using the habitable-zone formula above, the square root of 50 gives us a habitable zone distance of roughly 7 AUs. Again, being an evolved star, the habitable zone would be wider than that of a typical main-sequence star of comparable luminosity. Jupiter and Saturn would likely be in the present-day positions of Earth and Mars, allowing for slight expansion of their orbits due to mass-loss. Jupiter’s moons, likely burned to a crisp during the earlier RGB, would probably be lifeless and devoid of water. Enceladus, depending on how much water was lost, may stand a chance. Even so, I would say the best bet would be to go back to Titan. You see, with the red giant Sun having dimmed substantially, Titan would see another stint of habitability, the latter lasting a good 100 million years before the Sun enters its final stage of development, the AGB stage. The AGB stage happens when the Sun runs out of helium, during which it swells substantially, much like what happens during the RGB stage. But this time, owing partly to the fact that helium is a heavier element than hydrogen, the Sun will swell even more, brightening to a good 5,000 times the current luminosity toward the latter stages. This phase is much shorter than the RGB, only lasting about 20 million years compared to a billion for the RGB. Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and even Pluto will be too hot for habitability. The habitable zone here will also be increasingly unstable, due to random mass loss events and fluctuations in brightness that would make today’s sun cycle seem like a mere breath of wind. Only objects in the deep Kuiper belt would stand a chance, but much like Enceladus may, they could lose all of their water if a substantial atmosphere is unable to take hold. Most everything we know of today would be unrecognizable. Earth as a planet would cease to exist, fated to be engulfed during this latter AGB stage. While the Sun will cool from this AGB stage, the cooling will be permanent as after this stage, there will be no more fuel for the Sun to burn. The Solar System would thus be cast into eternal darkness, not a chance of habitability anywhere. In short, the last run of habitability during the red giant phase would be a last gasp for our local system, a shadow of what it once was in its heyday. Being so far in the future though, I wouldn’t worry about it. There are far greater things to worry about, like an orange man in the White House for example.

Question: What if Exoplanet HD984b was in the place of Jupiter? What implications would that have for Earth?
Answer: Thanks for the A2A. If HD 984 b existed in our solar system, we may not be here to know about it, especially if it orbited within Solar System scale distances. The object HD 984 b is so massive that when compared to the lowest mass stars, it is only about 15–20 percent less massive. At 65 Jupiter masses, it dwarfs everything that we know of in the solar system, Jupiter included. To get an idea of how big this thing is, if you took the entire mass of everything in the solar system and bunched it together into a planet, you’d still have another 63.5 Jupiter masses to go roughly. For the sake of this question, let’s replace Jupiter with HD 984 b where Jupiter is, at 5.2 AUs, and see what it looks like compared to Jupiter. Despite the mass being 65 times greater, due to gravitational contraction, the object will actually be slightly smaller than Jupiter, perhaps around 0.8 to 0.9 Jupiter radii. Internal heat would be insane, making storms like the Great Red Spot seem like a mere gust of wind. In fact, even at 4.5 Gyr, I’d dare say that the object would still glow like a lamp, probably being somewhere between 800–1200K. It would likely be the brightest object in the night sky, exceeding the apparent magnitudes of everything else. The current Jupiter has an apparent magnitude of roughly -2.5. Imagine how much brighter a Jupiter that glows red would be? It is safe to say the four Galilean moons would probably be destroyed at the relatively short distances they orbit at, or at the very least, be flexed to a volcanic crisp like Mustafar. But for an object the size of HD 984 b, the potential mass range of a satellite would exceed anything we know of. Moons the size of Earth, Uranus and Neptune, or even Saturn could form. The planet Kepler-1625b has a candidate moon the size of Neptune, and its total mass is “only” 10 Jupiter masses, or roughly one-sixth that of HD 984b, so who knows how much larger a potential satellite of HD 984 b could get? The Extrasolar Planet Encyclopaedia. Any potential satellite larger than Earth would be easily visible with the naked eye, so we’d have that going for us in terms of star-gazing. But alas, star-gazing would be the least of our worries if orbiting alongside an object like HD 984 b. The current Jupiter affects the orbits of the other planets in the Solar System via slight tugs, but the effects are small enough not to be noticeable in the long-term. The planets of the Solar System are spaced out enough for there not to be any issues. But with HD 984 b, the gravitational energy would be far greater than Jupiter. It is safe to say that the slight tugs by Jupiter would be replaced by something far greater and far worse. Instead of slight tugs, the effects of HD 984 b would be more akin to a grab and a push. Forget not noticeable. Within a few years, we’d notice tilting and alteration of ours and probably every other object in the Solar System. Stable orbits would slowly be sped up or slowed down, changing the courses of said objects. Obviously, with the differing orbits, masses, and distances, the tilting of each planet would not be uniform. Some may end up in higher orbits, others in lower. Inevitably, you’d get one planet to cross the orbit of another, and before long, you’d have the entire solar system in a mad game of planetary pinball. Some planets may collide, others tossed out of the Solar System, others flung into the Sun, etc. Earth among many others would very likely be tossed out of the Solar System within an astronomically short timescale. Perhaps a few lucky ones would end up in torch orbits around the Sun or uber-eccentric orbits that more resemble comets than planets, but the Solar System as we know it would forever be altered. Eventually, the only thing remaining in a stable orbit would be the gravitational bully that initiated the chaos and its moons. Such is the way of things. Its orbit would stay largely the same, perhaps a little altered by any collisions or ejections of other planets, but from its perspective, nothing much would change except from the fact that it would be the only planetary object left in the Solar System. And that is the way it would be for the foreseeable future. In any case, we wouldn’t be around to know it, so it wouldn’t make a difference to us.

Question: I have heard people call Jupiter a "failed star" that just did not get big enough to actually become a star, why didn't Jupiter become a star?
Answer: Contrary to what some people may say, Jupiter is not a failed star. It is a gas giant planet, a type of planet which we now know to be fairly common throughout the universe. Gas giant planets range anywhere between 0.3 to 60 times the mass of Jupiter. Now, before you nitpick this answer as being incorrect (some definitions for gas giants only include objects below 13 Jupiter masses), in 2016, a paper by co-authors Hatzes and Rauer came up with a definition to generalize all giant planets and brown dwarfs, due to the relative absurdity of classifying a 12.99 Jupiter mass object different from an otherwise identical 13.0 Jupiter mass object, simply because one is above an arbitrary line defined by humans. The general consensus was that objects between 0.3–60 Jupiter masses would be classified as gas giants, due to the fact of their similar radii and chemical composition, i.e, being composed of hydrogen and helium. [1506.05097] A Definition for Giant Planets Based on the Mass-Density Relationship. Both the Extrasolar Planets Encyclopaedia and the Open Exoplanet Catalog have been using this definition since, and every astronomer I know prefers this definition against the other. Whether you do or not is up to you, but for the purpose of this answer, we will use Hatzes and Rauer’s definition. Anyways, as massive as Jupiter is, you can clearly see from the paper above that the mass range of a Jupiter-like gas giant could potentially far exceed that of Jupiter, by a factor of 60 in extreme cases. Take the planet HD 984b for example. Here is a link. The Extrasolar Planet Encyclopaedia. Imagine if this planet existed in our solar system instead of Jupiter? If you thought Jupiter was huge, imagine something 65 times heavier. I won’t even go into the implications that would have on the orbit of Earth. Even still, an object like HD 984 b is not massive enough to be a star. Why? A true star would need a mass of some 80–85 times the mass of Jupiter. At the relatively light mass of 1 Jupiter, or even 65 Jupiters, the object is not massive enough to generate the heat required to begin nuclear fusion. Sure, the internal heat from contraction is there, but this is far from the heat generated by a star fusing via nuclear fusion. If we were to classify Jupiter on the Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram, it would fall into the category of Y-dwarfs, the lowest class which we currently know of. Brown dwarf - Wikipedia. The coldest brown dwarfs are somewhere between Y2-Y3. Jupiter would be somewhere around Y6 dwarf, so not even bright enough to beat the coolest objects we know of. An object like HD 984b, assuming an age of 4.5 Gyr, would likely be of class T, still well below that of the smallest stars. The point here is that stars are massive objects. While Jupiter may rightfully seem like a huge planet, it is still puny compared to even the smallest M-dwarfs like Barnard’s Star or Proxima Centauri. And that’s not even taking into account more massive stars like the Sun, Sirius, Betelgeuse, and beyond. Imagine what Jupiter would look like compared to something like R136a1? R136a1 - Wikipedia. It would no longer be us asking if Jupiter was a failed star.

Question: Why do gas giant planets not form closer to their star?
Answer: Actually, they do. The original theory was that there is not enough material close in to the star to facilitate the formation of a giant planet close to the star. However, in recent years, we have found thousands of giant planets close and snug to their stars in regions where we’d never expect to find them. True, it is likely that the methods we use to find them are biased toward close in planets, but as there is such a large number we have discovered, it is likely that some or maybe most of them have formed close in where they are currently located today. A good way to determine where they formed is the presence or lack of companions. If a hot Jupiter forms close to the star, it will likely form from a rocky core perhaps 5–15 times the mass of Earth before accreting a gaseous envelope that allows it to become the mass of Jupiter or greater. The rocky core will likely be formed alongside several other rocky cores, which may or may not become gas giants themselves. We’ve seen a number of planetary systems containing several planets in the 5–15 Earth mass range that orbit all within the orbit of Mercury and Venus. Take this system for example The six planets, all of masses between 2–20 Earth masses, orbit within a distance that would place them at or within the orbit of Mercury. Now, how does a system like Kepler-11 relate to the idea of close-in formation of gas giants? The idea is that in some of these systems, (yes, there are many others like Kepler-11), one or two of these planets would accumulate enough gas to become bona-fide gas giants. The rest would then stay as they are, and orbit the star in a collection of mini-Neptune/super-Earths and giant gas planets like Jupiter. A good example of such a system is WASP-47, which contains one hot Jupiter, a pair of Super-Earths/Neptunes, and a giant planet that orbits roughly between the distances of Earth and Mars. This is an example of a system where the close-in planet likely formed as a super-Earth/Neptune sized planet and then later on accumulated a substantial gas envelope that allowed it to become the size of Jupiter. Much as with the Kepler-11 system, two Neptune-sized planets that did not become gas giants closely sandwich the giant planet that orbits the star every three days. The only difference between this system and Kepler-11 is the fact that instead of two or more additional planets of 5–15 Earth masses, the WASP-47 system contains a single gas giant that accumulated most of all the material that the additional planets in the Kepler-11 system did not. Now, there is another type of close-in giant planet that forms much differently, and usually, the way to tell this one from the other is the lack of companions and a mis-aligned or eccentric orbit. This type of gas giant forms much farther out, at the distances where Jupiter and Saturn would be, then later migrates inward due to interactions between other planets, the planet-forming disk, and the star itself. Usually, it will form alongside several other planets of comparable mass, sometimes larger. This is because at far distances, material to form gas giants is much more abundant. Now, because the planet and its companions are so massive and moving all over the place, the formation of this planet is much more chaotic, involving ejections, collisions, gravitational slingshots, the like. The reason for lack of companions is because they are all ejected or have been destroyed. In essence, the lone hot Jupiter we see is the survivor of this planetary game of pinball. The planet HAT-P-7b is a great example of a planet like this. In this case, the planet actually orbits in a retrograde direction, meaning the opposite direction it actually should be orbiting in. This is a key indicator that it interacted with one or more planets, which have likely been ejected or destroyed. The lone hot Jupiter is the survivor, lonely without companions unlike its more peaceful counterparts. This type of system would be near impossible to form with a close-in and peaceful formation, since the hot Jupiters counterparts are likely to be a factor of 10 or more times less massive than in the latter scenario. The formation of giant planets is a complex process that is still being researched. More info to come in the future.

Question: What is the best case of beginner's luck you've ever had?
Answer: When I was 7 years old, I’d very recently taken up golf. Now, as most 7-year olds do, I was limited to the hit and giggle sessions on the range, as most beginner kids are. Now, I’ve never really been a big fan of hitting on the range for hours upon hours, even today. Usually, I limit range sessions to swing maintenence and warm-up balls, unless I’m at a course that has Prov1s on the range or something. But when I was 7, hitting on the range was all I knew, and as such, I quickly grew bored of the game. Fortunately for me, my parents quickly saw what was happening and signed me up for some on-course lessons with a pro. I immediately had a blast, realizing that there was more to this game than I thought. On my second time out with the pro, we came to a relatively short par 3. About 123 yards long, it was perfect distance for me to hit my 3-wood. I teed up the ball about an inch off the ground, then set up to hit it. “Alright matey, let this baby fly,” the pro said. I laughed. “Ok!” I agreed. I took the club back as far as I could, then let it rip as hard as possible for my 7-year old frame. When I connected, I immediately knew it was good, feeling the ball meet dead center on the clubface. The ball rocketed off into the distance, making a beeline at the flag. My heart thumped, suddenly realizing what a good shot I’d hit. “Oh wow, be right!” The pro yelled at the ball. We watched it land in the middle of the green, hop once, then roll softly toward the cup, eventually stopping about a foot from the hole. “That was awesome kid, way to go!” The pro high-fived me, my face beaming with pride. Stoked beyond belief, I sprinted toward the green with my putter in hand, realizing that on just my second time out, I would have my first birdie. I pulled the flag, then proceeded to make the one-foot putt for birdie, a wave of euphoria swallowing me like it would a surfer in the ocean. Immediately, I knew I was hooked into the game, realizing that this was what I wanted to do with my life. 11 years later, I am playing for a Division 1 college and am closer than I’ve ever been to making the PGA Tour. Perhaps none of this would have been possible without that amazing stroke (pun intended) of beginner’s luck.

Name: Andrew Chin
Question: Has a professional golfer ever cheated?
Answer: I personally have witnessed an incident of cheating by a professional golfer. In 2016, I was playing in a local state open with a former PGA Tour player who we’ll call “D” and a young upcoming mini-tour professional who we will call “B”. Now, before I proceed with the rest of the story, let me add a detail or two about B. B had spent the past two years or so trying to qualify for the Japan Tour. But in mysterious circumstances, he’d left Japan rather abruptly to return home, hence the reason he was playing in the state open. Of course, rumours were crossing the waves like fish in the ocean. These rumours included, but were not limited to allegations of cheating, shady rule breaches, and an ugly brawl with an official who reportedly banned him for life from the Japan Tour for cheating. Now, the entire field including myself had heard about the rumours, but since I was also playing alongside D, who was a former PGA Tour pro, I assumed everything would run smoothly, and if not, D would back me up. When game time rolled around, I made a mental note to myself to keep an eye on B. During the first round on the second hole, upon reaching the green after hitting our approach shots,”B” bent over to mark his ball, which was sitting on the edge of an old hole, picked it up quickly, then threw the coin on the side, about two inches closer to the hole, upon which he moved the ball to the coin’s new location about two inches away from the original spot. Of course, the ball was now conveniently away from the old hole, sitting pretty with an unobstructed view of the cup. B proceeded to make the four-foot putt for par, then proceeded to the next tee without incident. Now, initially, I did not notice what he did, but after “D” putted out, I noticed him stalking quickly to a pair of rules officials watching the action by the next tee. I realized we had a likely rules infraction, and decided to play it cool to see what would happen. Now, much to my chagrin, nothing happened for the remainder of the round, leaving me in the dark as to what had happened on the 2nd green earlier that afternoon. But after I putted out on 18 for a disappointing 73, “D” quickly pulled me to the side. Here was our conversation. D: “Hey, Andrew, real quick, I have to tell you something.” Me: “Yeah sure, what’s up?” D: “Now, I’m not sure if you noticed, but earlier on number 2, I noticed “B,” doing something very peculiar. Me: “Uh-huh, tell me more.” D: “Basically, I saw him put the coin down to mark it, then quickly throw it on the side closer to the hole.” “D” shook his head in disgust. Me: “So basically, you’re saying you saw him inch-worming?” D: “Yes, exactly. I’m going to confront him in the scoring tent. Now, I don’t want to do this, but as a former PGA Tour player, it is my duty to protect the field. You don’t need to say anything, and I will make sure that “B” knows it is me confronting him, not you. Me: “No problem, I understand.” As we entered the scoring tent, I nodded to “D” to encourage him. As D was marking B’s card, it was easier for him, since once he got the scores down, he left the space for the 2nd hole blank, highlighting the incident on the green. Of course, B noticed it was blank, and asked D to write down the score. D smiled, shaking his head. D: “B, is there anything you’d like to tell me about the 2nd green?” D gave him a knowing look. B, slightly confused, shook his head. D: “B, I’ve been on the Tour for several years, been around this game for almost my whole life. On number 2, I noticed when you marked your ball, you marked it in a very peculiar manner.” D raised his head, gesturing to me to borrow a ball. I threw the ball to him. D: “B, when you marked your ball, you were on the edge of an old hole. Do we all agree?” I nodded my head. D: “And when you unmarked it, you were suddenly a good two inches away from the old hole. Now, how does that happen?” D asked. Boom, bomb dropped. B shook his head slowly, face flushing, then said, B: “I remember what you said about number 2, and it is very disturbing to me what you are accusing me of. When I mark my ball, I mark it with the coin facing up, then when I placed it back, then I mark it with the coin facing down.” B recoiled a little, obviously struggling to come up with an explanation of what he did. But D was not done. D: “You still didn’t answer my question. Tell me. How does your ball end up a good two inches away from where it was?” D placed the ball on the table, then demonstrated to the scoring officials what he thought happened. B: “Like I said, I place the coin facing up, and when I unmark it, I place it with the coin down. I find it hard to see how that would happen. I don’t remember doing that at all.” D: “You still didn’t explain how the ball ended up off the face of the old hole. Do you remember Andrew?” D asked me. I raised my hands. Me: “I remember him being on the edge of an old hole, and after that, he was suddenly on the flat. Other than that, I don’t remember much, because I wasn’t paying that much attention. I was on the other side of the green.” D nodded, shaking his head in disgust at B. D: “B, like I said, I’ve been on Tour for a number of years. I’ve seen most everything, and bullshit like this is untolerable. I have no choice, but I am not going to sign this card. I heard the rumours from Japan, and although I initially did not believe them, I now find them to be somewhat true. It is disappointing for me, and I apologize, but it is my duty to protect the field. I can’t sign a card I know is not right. It is unfair to me, unfair to Andrew, and unfair to the 200 other guys who went out there and earned a score today.” He passed the card to the official, who nodded, then grimaced. Official: “I understand the allegations, and appreciate you D, and Andrew, for your inputs. Now, I have heard the rumours from Japan too, and while they are only rumours, we as the Committee will use the judgement of the whole panel to determine what, if any, penalties are assessed. Now, Andrew, you being on the other side of the green, your testimony is still appreciated, but as you were quite far, and not paying full attention, we may have to rely solely on D’s testimony. Andrew, you are free to leave, but D and B, you must stay, and we will discuss further. D smiled at me, shook my hand, and said, “See you tomorrow.” I quietly grabbed my things and left the two of them to discuss further what would happen. But inside, my mind was raging, having realized that the world of professional golf was not as squeaky clean as I thought it was. True, it was one of the most honest sports out there, but as with all professional sports, there were bound to be rotten apples. Myself having just witnessed an incident of incredible magnitude, this incident was likely to stick with me for the rest of my playing career. As a 17-year old amateur at the time, it was quite an experience to go through that and changed my perspective on the sport forever. Although B was eventually absolved of wrongdoing due to lack of sufficient evidence (there were no cameras on our group), the verdict on the street was that he had cheated. The next morning on the range, practically the entire 200 person field had heard the incident. D and I were the subject of many questions. Practically everybody wanted to know of what happened. Eventually, the fever pitch drama did die down, but B’s reputation was tarnished forever. Practically the entire range shunned him when he showed up to warm-up. I can’t imagine how he must have felt, but realize that he did it to himself. After all, it always pays to play fair, especially when your livelihood depends on beating other people for a paycheck. In essence, that was my story of witnessing a professional golfer cheat. It is sad to say, but golf is not immune from rotten apples. Wherever there is a big payoff, there are bound to be rotten apples. As with every other sport, there are bound to be folks looking to exploit every advantage to get what they want. Golf is no different.

Question: If planets were as big as stars would they have the same gravitational suction as stars?
Answer: Not necessarily. Remember that gravitational pull is determined by mass and not radius. By big, I assume you mean radius. There are many hot Jupiter planets that have similar or greater radii than many red dwarf stars. The reason for that is currently suspected to be a combination of extreme heat, tidal forces, and low mass. Take this planet as an example. Or this one Both of these planets have radii exceeding 2 Jupiters, and that is enough to have a jump on many M-dwarf stars such as our nearest neighbour Proxima Centauri. But while their sizes are phyiscally bigger than these stars, they contain much less mass. The planet on top, HAT-P-67b, has a radius of 2.09 Jupiters despite only having a mass of 0.34 Jupiters. This would make it’s total gravity well roughly equivalent to that of Saturn, which has 0.3 Jupiters worth of mass. So if you had a moon in orbit, it would seem like it was orbiting the planet Saturn. This is much less than a bona fide star such as Proxima Centauri which easily contains over 100 Jupiters. And the surface gravity of this planet would be even less. Because gravitational pull is determined by distance at an inverse proportion, the large radius of the planet would make the surface gravity a measly 0.21gs. This is compared to over 100gs for the surface of Proxima Centauri. Even Mars, which has a surface gravity of roughly 0.38g, is roughly two times stronger than this planet in terms of surface gravity. The planet on the bottom is slightly heavier, weighing in at 0.94 Jupiters, but this still makes the total gravity well slightly less than that of Jupiter, which by the way is quite far from becoming a star. And with a radius of 2.04 Jupiters, its surface gravity is still less than that of Earth, clocking in at 0.599g. So no, a planet as large as a star wouldn’t neccessarily have a similar gravitational pull. I should also mention that the heavier you make a planet, the smaller it’s radius will become, at least in terms of gas giants. If the two planets above instead of being 0.3 and 0.9 Jupiter masses were 30 and 90 Jupiter masses instead, their radii would not nearly be as bloated as they are now. Instead, they would only be roughly the size of Jupiter, due to the Kelvin-Helmoltz mechanism keeping the size in check. But then, they wouldn’t really be considered planets being that heavy. Which brings me to my last point.

Question: If Jupiter were to become a star, as theorized in Arthur Clarke's Odyssey Two, how would it affect planet orbits in our Solar System?
Answer: They’d probably all get ejected or destroyed. Jupiter is a large planet. 317.85 Earth masses, roughly 11 times the radius, more mass than the rest of the planets combined, etc. But in terms of star sizes, it is puny. To simply get it massive enough to start nuclear fusion, you’d have to add at least 80 times the mass it currently has. So, for the purpose of this question, let’s assume that Jupiter has 80 times the mass it currently has at its current distance from the Sun. At 5.2 AUs, it is not that far from the inner planets. Even today, Jupiter’s gravitational pull affects the orbits of all the planets. Imagine what something 80 times the mass would do? Something the size of Earth would have almost no chance. Initially, the orbits would trend slightly in the direction of the now magically 80 Jupiter mass object. As it cruised along in orbit, it would tow the orbits of the inner planets along with Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune as if they were tugboats in the wake of a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier. Minor disruption would be noticed, and seasons on Earth may get much more extreme. But as time went on, one would notice that seasons are the last thing we’d be worried about. As things go, the more massive an object is, the deeper it’s gravity well is. While the Sun’s gravity well is huge, an object with 80 Jupiter masses orbiting smack dab in the middle of everything would sure wreak havoc on everything in between and more. Some planets may get slingshotted out of the Solar System. Others may crash into the Sun. A few lucky ones may end up captured in orbit as moons, flung into a torch-orbit around the Sun, or in an orbit near where Planet 9 may be. Earth would almost certainly cease to exist as we know it today, either destined to spend the rest of eternity as a frozen starless world, or roasting up close to the Sun. We’d almost certainly die along with everything else that lives on this planet. In short, it would not be good. While two Suns may be a cool prospect, we wouldn’t live very long to see it.

Question: What was your most humiliating experience?
Answer: When the girl I asked to prom shut me down through text. Story time: For my senior prom, I decided to ask a girl in the grade below me to prom. She was quite popular, and I’d been waiting for this moment for a long time. We knew each other as friends/acquiantances, but previously, I’d been too shy to ask her out. I was a bit of a chicken in my younger days, but as prom neared closer, I decided to rid myself of the chicken-shit and ask her out on Valentine’s Day. Now, bear in mind that I’d never had a girlfriend, never asked out anybody, never even put myself out there. From my point-of-view, I was sticking my neck out much higher than I liked it. Call it fear of rejection. But I reasoned myself, if I never tried, I’d never get fruit, and what you don’t know can’t hurt you until you know it. Valentine’s Day rolled around, and I scrambled myself through the door. I’d hand-crafted a sign for two hours the night before, and struggled not to bend it as I drove to school. On the way, I stopped at a flower shop, buying a small rose and a balloon. For the rest of the morning, my mind was a blur as I figured out how I was going to ask her, where to find her, whether someone else would ask her, whether she’d say yes or no, whether I’d be ridiculed or not, you-know, the whole nine-yards. But what I knew was that I wasn’t going to chicken out. I was going to do it, and if I got rejected, then so be it. I was going to find her during homeroom, and pop the question there. Homeroom rolled around too soon for my shaking palms. Inside, I was a nervous mess. But outside, I played the part of a cool suitor, a man who knew what he wanted, and a guy ready for the big moment. I opened the door, and saw her walking across the quad. Perfect, I thought. I sprinted up the path to catch up with her. Me: “Hey!” I said. Her: “Hey Andrew, how are you?” Me: “Could you do me a favor?” Her: “Sure!” Me: “Will you be my Valentine at prom?” I dug out the rose and the balloon, and the sign, and handed them to her. She put her hands to her lips, obviously surprised, but smiled. Her: “Yeah, when is it?” Me: Tells her date and time Her: “Yeah, I think I will go!” Me: “Awesome! Could we grab a quick pic for the instagram maybe?” I fumbled around for my phone. Her: “Sure! Here, my friend will take it.” She handed the phone to her friend. Friend: “Smile!” Me & her: “Thanks!” We hugged each other. Me: “I got class now, but maybe we can grab lunch later or something!” Her: “Yeah, let me know!” I jogged off to homeroom, giddy as a lamb in a new field, and higher than the highest peaks. I made a few keyboard swipes, tagged her in the photo, then hit “send.” Awesome. Within seconds, people had seen the photo and were congratulating me. An hour later, I was sitting in stats class still giddy when I got the text: “Hey Andrew, really sorry that I couldn’t be honest, but I don’t think I can make it. I don’t think I know you well enough, but hope you can find somebody else. Thanks.” Instantly, I’d fallen from the peaks of Mt. Everest into the bottom of the Marianas Trench. I was crushed, both metaphorically and physically. To make matters worse, my photo had already garnered 80+likes, making for all the more humiliation. Practically the entire school was going to find out of what happened. Now, I was going to have to reverse everything, explain to everybody what had happened, and go hide myself until the storm blew over. Fortunately, my friends were all understanding and real supportive, but nothing could match the feeling of utter humiliation that I felt in those two minutes after I got that text. Immediately, I realized why relationships were so difficult, so time-consuming, and sometimes so heart-breaking. And the best/worst part? It was only a freakin prom-posal. Imagine what a real break-up or failed marriage proposal feels like? *Shudders P.S: It worked out in the end anyways as we both found different dates.

Question: Is a 62 on a par-70 course not as significant as a 62 on a par-72 course?
Answer: It depends. Most people who say that would argue that because a 62 on a par 70 is only 8 under, it is not as good as shooting 10 under for a par 72. However, on most par 70 courses, you also have the issue of having two less par 5s. PGA Tour pros make a large chunk of their scoring on par 5 holes, often scoring birdies and eagles on them, so it is arguable that a par 70 course is actually harder, because you don’t have the two extra par 5s to make eagles. If you think about it this way, “perfect” par 5 play for a Tour-level golfer would mean eagling all the par 5s. This means that a par 72 course with par 5s ranging between 550–630 yards has 4 potential eagle chances, while a par 70 course with the same length par 5s only have two eagle chances. If some hypothetical Tour pro had perfect play on the par 5s of a par 72, he’d be 8-under already, whereas if the same guy eagled both par 5s on a par 70, he’d only be at 4-under. For the par 70 course, this means the same golfer has to come up with 4–6 other birdie holes while on the 72, “perfect” par 5 play would mean that a golfer would only need to stiff a couple approach shots, maybe on a par 3 or short par 4 and you’d be at the number already. Personally, I prefer the par 72 course because of the extra birdie and eagle opportunities. Tour caliber par 70 courses often have many long par 4s that push the 500 yard mark, where simply making a par would feel like you gained a half-shot on the field, and birdies would almost be unheard of. Based on that, I’d say a 62 at a par 70 is arguably more impressive.

The present day Ko’olaus make up the Ko’olau range, rising about 2–3,000 feet above sea level. It is believed that the rift zones of the Ko’olau volcano ran parallel with the Nu’uanu Pali, a scar from a giant landslide that ravaged the island some 1 million years prior. This “pali or cliff” runs all the way from Makapu’u to Pupukea, basically the length of the whole island. The scarp of the Nu’uanu Pali is not the actual scarp from that landslide, but rather a result of the landslide weakening rocks on the windward side and making them more susceptible to erosion. A caldera is located near downtown Kailua, wrapping all the way ftom Lanikai to the Kaneohe Bay Area. Relicts from the ancient caldera include Mt. Olomana. You may be wondering about the famous cinder cones like Diamond Head and Punchbowl. While the general population says those are the volcanoes of Oahu, this is not technically accurate as these cinder cones are merely satellites of the much larger Ko’olau range. When the Ko’olau volcano was in its last phase of development it underwent a period known to geologists as the rejuvenated stage. For almost 500,000 years, it went through a period of no activity before having one last hurrah. Isolated pockets of magma stuck underneath the volcano blasted through the crust sporadically, with intervals between explosions sometimes as great as 100,000 years. At least ten, and likely up to 50 of these eruptions occured, with eruption sites ranging from the lesser known offshore areas near Kaneohe Bay all the way to the famous cones such as Diamond Head and Punchbowl. No pattern in the eruption has been found except for several eruptions near the Koko Head area that seem to follow loosely the old rift zones. The volcano may still have some activity left as the last eruption near Makapuu was only about 10,000 years ago. On the west side of Oahu is Waianae volcano, also a deeply eroded shield volcano about 3.9 million years old. A former caldera exists in Lualualei Valley. Unlike the Ko’olau, Waianae seems to have had no rejuvenate activity, and much of the known eruption sites are either from the shield or post-shield stages of development. The Waianae volcano was once as high as 12,000 feet above sea level, somewhere in between the present day Haleakala or Mauna Kea volcanoes in height and size. Because the Ko’olaus block much of the rain, the Waianae side is very dry, with erosion processes happening somewhat slower than over at the Ko’olaus. Not many people know, but Oahu actually has a third volcano, called Kaena. Located west of Waianae, it is underwater now, but in the past, rose almost 4,000 feet above sea level. At 5.1 million years old, it is the oldest of Oahu’s volcanoes, but may still be undergoing the rejuvenated stage. A submarine eruption in 1956 is thought to coincide with the location of this underwater volcano, although no evidence has been found since the mountain was discovered in 2014. If you’re looking for active volcanoes, you may want to visit Hawaii island instead, where Kilauea volcano has erupted continously since 1983. Oahu’s volcanoes are all dead or nearly so, but still make good hiking spots!

Question: Can a pilot learn to fly more than one plane?
Answer: Sure. On Airbus aircraft, there is a concept of cockpit commonality, meaning that the flight decks of the A320, A330, A340, A350, and A380 are common enough to facilitate differences training and mixed-fleet flying between aircraft families within several days. The three wide-bodies in the middle, the A330, A340, and A350, can be operated as one line with pilots flying all three aircraft types in a common pool. An example of an airline that does this is Lufthansa. Although there are slight differences in the A350 vs the A330/A340, (HUD and a 6-pane windscreen vs 4 in the former come to mind) the A350 was granted a common type-rating with the A330. The A340 is operated under a separate clause of mixed-fleet flying, likely due to the differing amount of engines, 4 in a 340 vs 2 in a 330/350. By this same vane, Airbus airline pilots can utilize mixed fleet flying to operate a number of different aircraft not excluded to the A330, A340, and A350. I know of several airlines in Europe and at least one in the Middle East who operated the A320 series and the A330 in a common pool for a number of years. While it is theoretically possible, I do not know of any airlines who fly both the A330/A350 and the A380 as a common pool, but I could be wrong, so anybody out there who knows better, feel free to correct me! Over on the Boeing side, the 757 and 767 families share a common type-rating as both aircraft were developed concurrently as part of the same family. Slight differences between the two include obvious ones like the single aisle on the 757 vs the twin-aisle on the 767, and not so obvious ones like stepping down into a 757 cockpit vs stepping up on a 767. Still, airline pilots are able to fly both types, all the way from 757 freighter up to 767–400ER provided their airline actually operates the whole family. All the legacy US carriers operate the 757 and 767 as a common pool. The 777 and 787 families also share a common type rating, likely mirroring the A330 and A350 common type rating. Again, I do not fly either, so feel free to correct me if I am wrong. With nine days differences training, pilots are able to fly both in a mixed-fleet flying pool, much like their Airbus colleagues are able to fly the A330/340/350 in a common pool. I know of at least one airline in Asia that does this. And of course, one must not forget the test pilots that work at Boeing and Airbus. Many of them are rated on several aircraft models at the same time. It is not uncommon for a pilot at either company to fly say, an A321, an A330, an A380, and an A350 in the same month, or a 777, a 747, a 767, a 787, and a 737MAX in the same month. Not sure if this is the answer you were looking for, but hope this helps!

Question: Why does the Airbus A340 have 4 engines?
Answer: In the 1970s and 80s, Airbus wanted to enter the long-haul widebody market that Boeing had dominated for so many years with their 747 program. At this point in time, airlines were still subject to the regulation of stringent ETOPS regulations. ETOPS stands for Extended Twin Engine Operation Performance Standards. Note that ETOPS still exists today, but in the 70s and 80s, this regulation was much more strict. By strict, I mean that distances from land were limited to 90 and 120 minutes from a suitable diversion airport, not the incredible 350 and 420 minute ETOPS regs enjoyed by today’s A350 and B787. While 120 mins may seem like a lot, note that a relatively short flight like Honolulu to LAX would fall short under a 120 minute ETOPS rule. As such, twin jets were extremely limited, making it more economically profitable at the time to fly quadjets on long over water routes. Since quads were immune to ETOPS, they could fly as far away as they liked, taking a more direct route in favor of one that deviated and cost way too much in excess fuel. So Airbus decided to study the concept of a new twin-aisle program, using the fuselage of the A300, but with vast modifications. Provisionally, they dubbed this concept the TA-9 and the TA-11. The TA-9 was to feature twin-engines for short-medium haul operations like the A300, and the TA-11 was to feature four engines for long-haul operations. With a strengthened fuselage/landing gear, a common fly-by-wire cockpit with the TA-9, four engines, redesigned wing, and added fuel capacity, the TA-11 became the first true Airbus long-haul aircraft. Entering service in 1993, the TA-11 became known as the A340. Having the range to connect city pairs such as Hong Kong to Los Angeles, Singapore to Frankfurt, the airplane performed exactly how Airbus designed it to. However, there was a problem. In 1990, Boeing was showing the FAA how they could successfully operate an aircraft at 180 minutes ETOPS, even a brand-new one like the Boeing 777, which hadn’t even flown at the time. The FAA agreed, allowing the 777 180-minute ETOPS at its entry into service. Before long, Boeing was pushing the idea of the 777 as the new long-range aircraft, even going to the extent of offering to buy airlines’ rival A340s (Singapore) in exchange for new 777 aircraft. While sales for the A340 were drying up, sales for the 777 were only gathering momentum, and rightfully so. The 777, a masterpiece of an aircraft, had greater range than the A340 did, was generally more fuel efficient, and was cheaper to maintain. An aircraft like 777–200ER could fly from New York to Hong Kong nonstop, something the early A340s could do only with severe payload cuts. This pushed Airbus to develop the A340–500 and the A340–600. No problem for Boeing, as with several design tweaks and modifications, they were able to come up with the 777–300ER, the 777–200LR, and a freighter model. To make matters worse for the A340, the ETOPS regulations were only relaxed further, allowing the 777 to fly 240 and eventually 330 minutes from a nearby airport. The A340, four-engined for long-haul, was practically obsolete by the year 2010. Was this a failure for Airbus? Heck no. In lieu of the ETOPS relaxing and the success of the 777, Airbus’s own A330 enjoyed far more success than ever envisioned. Originally designed for short-medium haul operations, Airbus was able to raise the MTOW of the aircraft to give it true long-haul capabilities. Up from a range of 3,500nm, today’s A330s can fly up to 7,500nm at the longest-ranged variants. The A330 was also the first aircraft to enjoy ETOPS-240. While sales of the A340 have dried up, the A330 family has racked up over 1,300 sales and counting. Airbus, realizing how much they could tweak out of the A330 design, was able to improve the A330 to the point where it became the long-haul Airbus aircraft that everyone wanted. And with added benefit, the A330 enjoys a common cockpit with the A340, allowing for easier pilot training. All this boils down to the A330 and the A340 being part of a family that complements each other. To Airbus, their family succeeded, since sales of the 330 and 340 combined have garnered over 1,600 units. Is the 340 a lesser aircraft? Of course not. The 340 performed how it was designed to. It just came too little too late. Had the 340 flown in the late 70s, it could have racked up the sales Airbus was hoping it would.

Question: How do parents deal with false (scientific) facts being taught to your child in school?
Answer: I’m no teacher, but myself having recently graduated high school, am somewhat qualified to answer this question. When I was in elementary school, I was attending an extremely religious-based school. Now, by religious, I mean that I was threatened with detention for wearing a Buddhist necklace my grandfather gave me. As such, science was not exactly the most accurate in that place. One incident that still irks me to this day happened during a writing workshop thingamabob they had us do in 3rd or 4th grade. Our assignment was to write a story about a fictional event based off a real-life event. Myself, being the aviation geek I am, decided to write a story based on the real event of Air Transat 236, an Airbus A330 aircraft that ran out of fuel over the ocean, eventually gliding more than 100 miles to a safe landing in the Azores. In my story, I used an Airbus A340 instead of an A330, and instead of a fuel leak, I decided to make it a calculation error like the Air Canada Gimli Glider incident. Last but not least, instead of a safe landing in the Azores, the A340 in my story would ditch in the rough choppy seas. If this sounds like a big project for a 10-year old, well, it was. I wrote about a page of this thing before realizing that I had my hands full and that I should probably ask my teacher for help. Now, when I showed my teacher the notes I’d scribbled for my outline and the page I had written, instead of getting the assistance I needed, I was chastised for not following the assignment guidelines, threatened with lunch detention, and sent to start over. My crime? My story, real as it was, was deemed, “too unrealistic to ever happen, too violent for the context of a 4th-grade classroom, and too gory for a good Christian mind.” When I protested to my teacher that this in fact really did happen, she shook her head, saying there was no way an airplane could continue flying after running out of fuel, especially over an ocean like Air Transat did. I tried explaining to her the concept of the airplane retaining momentum but she wouldn’t budge. Claiming quite adamantly I was wrong and had no clue what I was talking about, she even threatened me with a trip to the principal’s office for questioning her knowledge of physics rather rudely, justified as I felt I was. I pleaded with her one last time, promising I would allow everyone to live, but she wouldn't have it. Instead, as punishment for causing so much trouble, she assigned me a topic about “fairy-pixies,” since I was so adamant about writing a “fantasy piece.” Sullen and defeated, I returned to my seat in the computer lab and started typing out a half-assed story about fairy pixies. Or at least I was pretending to. In secret, I was actually researching the concept of glide ratio and technique of dead-stick landings. While I was reading the biography of Captain Robert Piche, I pledged that I would never allow myself to naively believe wrong facts like my teacher must have done at some point in her life. Whenever I had a doubt, I would research something. As a former US president once said, “Trust, but verify.” The trust part is optional, since people like my former teacher shouldn’t be trusted. But the verification part? Since even the smartest people make mistakes, verification is mandatory. The top scientists and statisticians would agree with me. Always verify and double-verify your findings. If you, or any of your friends should encounter wrong-fact preachers in school like I did, teach your kids the concept of “Trust but verify.” In other words, take the teacher’s words with a grain of salt until you verify what they are telling you is true. It will go a long way for them.

Question: How do pilots keep their cool during emergencies?
Answer: You fall back on your training. There was a great Navy Seals quote I read somewhere. It said, “there is no such thing as rising to the occasion. When the shit hits the fan, you fall back on your training.” For the pilot in an emergency, this rings so true. There is no such thing as rising to the occasion. True, you may face things you might not see in the simulator. QF-32 was a great example. Hundreds of EICAS messages, warnings, multiple failures of critical systems, fuel leaks, etc. As one of the pilots put it, “It was a check-ride from hell.” But even during occasions such as these, you fall back on your training, your knowledge of the aircraft. Those four or three bars on your shoulder mean a lot in times of crisis. You’ve trained for thousands of hours in your life. As such, when the shit hits the fan, you don’t need to get all panicky. Sure, the odds may ever be stacked against you, as they were in the case of UAL 232, the DC-10 that lost all hydraulics. But even then, you rely on your training to get you out of the emergency. Those hours of experience. Those days when you took the Cessna into backwater airports. Those sleepless nights that you spent looking over the QRH or the emergency engine out checklist in order to pass your check-ride. They all come in handy when the shit hits the fan. If the emergency is too severe, perhaps you may not live. That is a possibility every pilot faces when he or she takes to the air. But when you have people behind you who entrust you with their lives, you’d rather die than let a single one of your passengers meet their maker on your watch. Every pilot I know shares this sentiment. As such, even in hopeless situations like JAL 123 or UAL 232, the pilots up front will struggle every inch of the way to ensure that as few lives as possible are lost, even if it means they lose their own.

Question: What were the similarities between Palpatine witnessing Anakin Skywalker vs Count Dooku, and Palpatine witnessing Darth Vader vs Luke Skywalker?
Answer: Anakin vs Dooku and Vader vs Luke are two very similar battles that bring the saga full circle. Although spread by the space of about 22 years, similar objectives are at hand. Palpatine, the all powerful Sith master, is grooming a new potential recruit. To test this recruit, he pits his old apprentice against this young and upcoming recruit. In Dooku’s case, the young recruit was Anakin, and in Vader’s case, the young recruit was Luke. I’m sure throughout the course of the battle, Anakin must have realized at some point that his master was looking to replace him with something far better and far more powerful, as he’d seen this game before. But because Palpatine is much more powerful than Anakin in the suit, Anakin has no choice but to fall in line or risk the ire of his master’s lightning. We all know how that turned out with Windu and Yoda. Palpatine is scared of his apprentices because of the Sith rule of two. Palpatine himself killed his master, Lord Plageuis, so he could become the master. Palpatine is not stupid and knows that at some point, his apprentice would try to replace him. In Dooku’s case, Dooku was already a very powerful Sith and could hold his own with great swordsmen like Obi-Wan and even Anakin himself. He trained a very powerful apprentice in Asajj Ventress who Palpatine ordered to be killed because she was getting to powerful. So Dooku certainly has potential to overthrow Palpatine. To take care of that problem? He has Dooku fight Anakin. Although Dooku has bested Anakin before, Anakin is young and strong, and certainly no pushover. Furthermore, during Anakin and Dooku’s battle, Anakin is close to the peak of his power. As such, Anakin bested Dooku, and beheaded him mercilessly at Palpatine’s urging. Now with Vader and Luke, the scenario is slightly different. Vader is now broken, from his injuries, from the humiliation, and is nothing more than a broken attack dog. Luke, his son, is whole, not injured aside from the hand he lost on Bespin, and has great potential, as we see when he defeats Vader one on one. In this battle, Palpatine aims to replace Vader with Luke, as 22 years ago, when Palpatine tried to replace Dooku with Anakin, he wasn’t counting on Anakin getting injured and falling in lava. He even said to Yoda during their battle, “Soon Lord Vader will be more powerful than either of us!” That plan was out the window once Vader fell in the lava. He was still incredibly strong, as we saw in Rogue One and the Original trilogy, but nowhere near as powerful as he could have been without his injuries. Post-injuries Vader couldn’t even shoot lightning because of his suit. Now with Luke, here was the apprentice that Palpatine sought after in the beginning, the one that he envisioned Anakin becoming. Sure, it was 22 years later, but better late than never. But the difference in this battle vs the Anakin Dooku one was that Luke refused to kill his father the way Anakin murdered Dooku. Despite Palpatine’s urgings, Luke refused to turn to the dark side and as such, became a true Jedi. This was the first domino that ultimately led to Palpatine’s death at the hands of Vader, who became redeemed when he became good again. Had Anakin taken the same choice as Luke did, the Sith may very well have been destroyed at the end of Revenge of the Sith. Ultimately, the two battles are very similar, with the latter taking a turn that ultimately leads to the redemption of Vader and the fall of the Empire. It comes pretty full circle in my opinion.

Question: What is the top speed of Boeing 777-300ER?
Answer: Most airplanes will have an optimum cruise speed between Mach 0.8-Mach 0.86 and a MMO or max mach number around Mach 0.9ish. The 777–300ER is no different. The speed you saw was due to strong tailwinds. With a strong tailwind, you might get a ground speed of 1200 km/h! Going the other way, your ground speed may be only 600 km/h. But Mach number is based off airspeed which is based off the speed that the airplane is flying through the air. In other words, the ground-speed has no effect on the airplane itself. You could have a headwind of 800km/h but if the plane is flying at 800km/h airspeed, it will still be flying at Mach 0.8 despite being at a standstill relative to the ground. In your case, you were lucky to have a strong tailwind as you probably arrived quite early.

Question: Can a commercial plane land without fuel?
Answer: Yes it can, but it is not advised. Still, it has happened several times in the past. One of the most famous involves Air Transat Flight 236, an Airbus A330–200 flying from Toronto to Lisbon Portugal. Halfway across the Atlantic, the aircraft experienced a fuel leak caused by an incorrect part in the hydraulic system that ruptured the fuel lines leading to the Number 2 engine. When the onboard computers sensed fuel imbalance, the pilots tried to trouble-shoot by cross-feeding fuel from the tanks on the left wing to the tanks on the affected engine, not knowing that there was a fuel leak. Alas, the jet ended up running out of fuel some 135 miles from the Azores. Still, Captain Piche and First Officer DeJager managed to glide the Airbus and land safely at Lajes Air Force Base. Despite popping eight of the plane’s 12 tyres, everybody survived that incident. Because of conservation of momentum laws, if an airplane loses power at cruising altitude ala Air Transat 236, the airplane will still continue to move forward, but will descend in altitude because of the lack of thrust powering the aircraft through the air. Still, it is not a question of where, but when the aircraft hits the ground when this happens.

Question: Why do airplane engines fail at high altitude?
Answer: This happens due to a lack of air. Jet engines breathe air, and above a certain altitude, there won’t be enough air to run the engine. Indeed, if you climb too high, the engines can and will shut off. There was a CRJ crash a few years back where the pilots had the aeroplane to themselves. They wanted to see what the limits of the plane were and tried climbing the plane to 41,000 feet which was the maximum approved altitude for said aeroplane. As the story goes, they made some critical blunders like climbing at an excessive rate at high altitude- I think they were climbing 500fpm all the way up to 41,000 feet which is way above the manufacturer’s maximum recommended climb rate above 38,000 feet- not maintaining enough airspeed, (they’d gotten down to about 150 knots indicated, which is barely above stall speed) and ignoring stall warnings from the plane’s computers which could have really saved their butts that day. So after the pilots overrode four automatic nose-down inputs from the flight computers, the engines shut off. They attempted to windmill restart it by putting it into a dive to gain the airspeed critical to a windmill restart. But because the engines had cooled too much, the assembly didn’t match and the blades couldn’t rotate freely. They were unable to restart the engines all the way down to the ground, when they realized far too late what had happened. Although there were 6 airports within reach of the plane, they were banking on being able to restart their engines and didn’t realize the inevitable until they were far too low and too late. They tried to glide their plane onto a well-lit road but ended up crashing behind some houses a couple miles from the airport. So in short, jet engines do shut off if you fly too high. Best not to exceed manufacturer standards as they are the ones who designed and built the thing.

Question: If a plane crash is imminent, are the passengers informed?
Answer: One of the most famous plane crashes in the United States was the crash of United Airlines Flight 232. United Airlines Flight 232 was a DC-10 flying from Denver to Chicago O Hare. When the aircraft was at its cruising altitude of 35,000 feet, a fan blade in the No.2 engine broke, causing an uncontained engine failure. In short, an uncontained engine failure is when the engine failure causes damage to the outer components of the engine. Usually, an uncontained engine failure causes said engine to explode. On this flight, the uncontained failure ruptured all three hydraulic lines which ran near the No.2 engine on the DC-10. When the hydraulics were ruptured, this caused the aircraft to become uncontrollable. Basic flight control features such as pitch, roll, yaw, etc were impossible. In fact, the only thing working for the flight crew were the engines. Imagine trying to fly an airplane using purely engine power. The three pilots, Captain Al Haynes, First Officer Bill Records, and Flight Engineer Dudley Dvorak, struggled to steer the plane using only engine power, juggling the throttles to make the asymmetric thrust turn the plane in a very slow wide right turn. It has been estimated that the odds of suffering such a complete systems failure are more than a billion to one. The odds of landing it safely? Don’t even get me started on that one. Because the plane couldn’t use its ailerons, elevators, rudders, or any other major control surface, not only was it difficult to fly straight, but to turn, descend, line up with a runway, and land it at an appropriate sink rate and flare was damn near impossible. Japan Airlines Flight 123 was another such incident, and in that incident, the plane ended up flying into a mountain after the pilots held on for 33 harrowing minutes. Anyhow, the flight crew enlisted the help of a DC-10 instructor, Denny Fitch, who also had no clue. Fitch helped with the throttles and essentially became a member of the crew. Obviously, the passengers had some inkling as to what was happening, but because the aviators code is “Aviate, navigate, and communicate,” an announcement to the passengers only happened just a few minutes before landing in Sioux City. In his announcement, Captain Haynes said, “ LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, THIS IS CAPTAIN AL HAYNES SPEAKING. AS YOU MUST BE AWARE BY NOW, WE'RE HAVING SOME CONTROL DIFFICULTIES WITH THE PLANE. WE'RE ATTEMPTING AN EMERGENCY LANDING IN SIOUX CITY. WE'LL BE LANDING IN APPROXIMATELY EIGHT MINUTES. WE'VE GOT ABOUT AS MUCH CONTROL OVER THE PLANE AS WE CAN GET, BUT I NEED YOU TO UNDERSTAND THIS IS GOING TO BE A CRASH LANDING. PLEASE REVIEW YOUR EMERGENCY PROCEDURES. THIS IS GOING TO BE WORSE THAN ANYTHING YOU'VE EVER BEEN THROUGH BEFORE, AND YOU NEED TO BE READY. WE WILL DO EVERYTHING IN OUR POWER TO GET EVERYONE TO THE GROUND, BUT WE NEED YOUR COOPERATION.” Obviously he wasn’t going to sugarcoat anything. Here he was, flying a crippled airliner that had absolutely no control whatsoever, and he had 288 other poor souls sitting behind him. As the pilot-in-command, you are responsible ultimately for the outcome of the flight. So you want your passengers to be as equipped as possible to survive such a crash. So Captain Haynes made it clear what was going to happen, to mentally prepare his passengers for the inevitable. Although Captain Haynes was not able to land the plane without fatalities, his actions no doubt saved hundreds of lives that day.

Question: In a jet plane, how do we get oxygen while at cruising altitude?

Question: How is it possible for planes to collide in mid air flight? What are some examples of this happening?
Answer: Usually errors by air traffic control and pilots are the culprit. In congested airspace, it is difficult for controllers to keep track of every single plane in the skies. One of the most notorious mid-air collisions involved a Saudia 747 and a Kazakh Ilyushin IL-76. At the time, Delhi airport had one air lane open to civilian planes only. The simple version is this: The Saudi 747 was climbing through 14,000 when it was asked to hold. The Kazakh was cleared to an altitude 1,000 feet higher as is standard practice. However, the Kazakh plane kept descending through its assigned altitude and ended up hitting the Saudi plane which was flying the other way. Factors which caused this: congested airspace and pilot error by the Kazakh crew. The controllers did not make a mistake here and it was the fault of the Kazakh crew. Today, planes have TCAS avoidance, or collision avoidance. It is very effective in preventing mid-air collisions. However, the Saudi plane did not have TCAS which could have otherwise prevented the crash. A notable crash involving TCAS happened with a DHL 757 and a Russian Tupolev 154. https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Überlingen_mid-air_collision In this case, TCAS told the Russian airliner to descend, and the controller, not realizing TCAS told the Russian airliner to descend, told the DHL plane to descend too. The DHL plane, which was supposed to climb via TCAS instructions, followed ATC instructions and descended right into the Russian plane. This was an example of the fault of the controller. However, mid-air collisions are quite rare and don’t happen all too often. In today’s day and age, technology is so sophisticated and pilots and controllers are so well trained that it is extremely unlikely that it will happen.

Question: Why can't we, as passengers, feel the speed when flying on-board an airplane?
Answer: By speed, you are most likely meaning acceleration. Yes, you can feel acceleration, just sit back and observe when your airplane is taking off. An airplane when taking off is accelerating through about 180mph, and by the time the pilots retract the gear, is probably travelling over 200mph. The period from take-off to cruise altitude is where the acceleration part of the flight occurs. Yes, you can definitely feel the acceleration, and you can definitely notice the plane is travelling faster and faster. Oh, but why doesn’t it look fast from my window? Well, as you get farther from the ground, the things on the ground become way smaller. The trees you see when driving through the cul-de-sac becomes swathes of green on the ground. Cars become ants, or fireflies at night. Eventually, when you reach cruising altitude, you are as much as 12 km away from the point on the ground below you, assuming that point is at sea level. Imagine if you are driving on the highway, a really long and open highway in Arizona or the desert part of California. If you are sitting in the passenger seat, you can likely see places that are as much as 12km away, if not more. Now, imagine that these things are the only thing you can see to determine your relative speed in the car. If using these far-off objects to determine your relative speed, your car will seem like it is barely crawling along. You may be driving at 80mph, but because these objects are so far away, you really can’t tell. The same effect happens with an airplane, except that the far-off object is usually the ground. If there are clouds, they may be used, since they are most definitely nearer to you than the ground, but then again, who drives alongside a cloud other than an airline or fighter pilot? When you reach cruising altitude, you will no longer feel acceleration, not because the ground objects are so far away, but because the aircraft is no longer accelerating! Aircraft fly at a constant speed and altitude, unless either taking off or descending. It is more practical and fuel efficient to fly at a constant speed and altitude rather than constantly climbing or descending. The only climbs or descents during the cruise phase of the flight may be because of separation problems, air traffic control stuff, turbulence/and/or weather, or step-climbs filed into the flight plan of a long-haul flight. But assuming the aircraft is in level 1G flight, it will feel as if you are on a stationary object on the ground, since the object is neither accelerating nor decelerating. Yes, aircraft tend to cruise in a slightly nose-up attitude, so you may notice that walking to the back of the aircraft is slightly downhill, but other than this, you wouldn’t feel amiss at all.

Question: What's the landing speed of a 747? Is it always the same?
Answer: The landing speed of a 747 or any aircraft depends largely on the weight of the aircraft at landing. A fully loaded 747 will be coming in faster than an empty 747 by about 40-50 knots. If you are talking about the ground-speed of the 747, that will also change, due to wind or atmospheric pressure. A Boeing 747 landing in Denver will have a higher ground speed than a 747 landing in Honolulu because the air is thinner at 5,500 feet MSL. Aircraft fly based on airspeed, so while the groundspeed will vary by quite a bit, the airspeed will generally be around the same. I couldn't give you an exact airspeed number again because of the different characteristics of every flight, but based on my X-Plane 10 numbers, the 747-400 likes to land at an airspeed of around 140-150 knots if it's at an acceptable landing weight (747 pilots, correct me if this number is wrong for whatever reason). If fully loaded, it'll be as much as 170 knots at times, but you don't ever land at MTOW unless an extremely rare emergency arises like an in-flight fire.

Question: What does a pilot say when he thinks he is going to crash?

Question: What happens if a plane doesn't gain enough airspeed to take off?
Answer: It won't get off the ground. Airplanes fly because of lift, and the high-speed air flowing across the wing generates this needed lift. If the airspeed is not high enough, the required lift won't be there, and the aircraft won't fly. It will keep rumbling along the runway until it gets the required airspeed/lift, or until it collides with something after overrunning the runway. There was an incident in 2009 where the scenario you described happened. The aircraft was an Airbus A340-500, flying from Melbourne to Dubai. On the A340, (A340 pilots correct me if I'm wrong) the pilots will input the takeoff weight to the flight computer allowing it to calculate the needed thrust for takeoff. This is standard procedure for flex takeoffs. The pilots made a mistake on the takeoff weight on the flight computer, putting a weight 100 tons lower than the actual takeoff weight. The first officer then changed the first digit on the flex takeoff weight, believing it to be transcribed incorrectly. As a result, the captain didn't detect the error. So when the aircraft began its takeoff roll, the thrust applied was insufficient to take-off. The result was that the plane took much too long to accelerate to takeoff speed. By the time it did, the airplane was already off the runway, and the pilots were desperately trying to avoid hitting the airport fence and a building at the end of the runway, dragging the tail along the ground in the process. But when the airplane finally got enough speed, it lifted into the air like it was supposed to. Airplanes are designed to fly based on lift, and without the lift that they need, they simply won't fly.
