Question: Can airplanes and jet fighters fly with no atmosphere?
Answer: First things first, all jet engines breathe air, so they will flame out due to lack of atmosphere. Furthermore, planes fly based on Bernoulli's principle of lift. The shape of the wing causes the air to move on top of the wing faster. This because in fluid dynamics, an increase in the speed of a fluid, causes a simultaneous decrease in the pressure of the fluid. This will cause the plane to climb, because objects in a fluid such as air like to go from high pressure areas to low pressure areas. You can observe the same effect by tying two soda cans slightly apart, and blowing air through the gap between the cans. Most would think the cans would fly apart, but due to Bernoulli's principle of lift, the cans are sucked together by the fast air moving through the gap. In the same sense, the aircraft is the soda can but on a much grander scale. The faster moving air on top of the airfoil will cause the plane to be sucked to the low pressure area. In the case of the plane, this means up, and the plane will achieve flight once the difference in pressure becomes greater than the pull of gravity on Earth. The net pull of all the forces acting on the plane is a pull towards the sky, and forwards due to the thrust being supplied. However, to generate the lift needed, you either need a really powerful wind, or a lot of thrust, hence the engine. Thrust is a huge part of the equation, and without thrust or some equivalent, you won't fly even in the atmosphere of Venus. Current jet engines such as the GE-90-115B or the CF6-50 breathe air, and flame out when faced with a lack of oxygen. If you could build a non-air breathing engine, powerful enough to power an object through the sky without the aid of an atmosphere, then this machine would be able to fly. This is how a rocket flies, because it has so much thrust that even though it looks nothing like an airplane should look, it is still able to fly because it has enough thrust. But I'm assuming your question only concerns commercial and fighter planes, not space planes.

Question: What are the safest seats on an airplane?

When the airplane hits the water, because you land without landing gear in the water, the back of the airplane will likely break off, killing everyone here. The guys in the front will survive if they don't drown. When an airplane catches fire, it's really a toss of the dice. Depending where the fire is coming from, it's probably best to sit far away from the fire. But in the event of a fire, you only have about 22 minutes to go from cruise to landing, so it won't really matter where you sit anyways. If the airplane explodes due to a fuel fire, it's best to sit away from the wings, where the fuel is stored. There are so many variables in determining the safest seat on an aeroplane. It really depends on the emergency and the crash.

Question: What would happen if a 747, A380 or any big passenger jet flew way too fast and broke the sound barrier?

If you flew even faster, the airplane will simply come apart. It is very stressful for an airplane to make that jump from Mach 0.98 to supersonic. In fact, when the 747-8 was undergoing flight tests, when it did the maximum speed test, the flight test crew noted the airframe being noticeably pushed to the limit. They experienced vibrations and flutter not normally seen in Mach 0.8 cruise. Airliners are not designed for supersonic flight, and designing one for supersonic cruise would require a lot of design changes, in the wings, the engines, fuselage and aircraft systems. It would be too costly to reengineer a 747 or A380 for that purpose.

Question: How high do jetliners fly?
Answer: Generally, airliners like to cruise between 30 to 43,000 feet. Notice the wide range I specified. A lot of factors can influence the cruising height of an airliner. The most important factor is the weight of the airplane. How much weight are we carrying? A heavier airliner won't fly as high for obvious reasons. Consequently, a Boeing 747 or 777 at MTOW may only be able to cruise at about 33 to 35,000 feet for the initial phase of the flight. Any higher and the airplane reaches the coffin corner. But because you burn fuel to carry fuel, the same airliner 6 hours later will be much lighter. The weight of the fuel can be as much as 40 percent of the total weight of the aircraft. So on a flight from HKG to JFK, you might takeoff with as much as 260,000lbs of fuel on a typical Boeing 777-300ER flight. But 6 hours later, you might only have about 150,000lbs left, because you burned a lot of fuel initially. Heavy aircraft and lower cruise altitude, equals more fuel burn. Because the airplane is now lighter, you can now climb to a higher altitude for a better fuel burn. So said 777-300ER can now climb to 37,000 feet instead of 35,000. This procedure is called a step-climb, and is routine for long flights. 5 hours later, you burned even more fuel. You now will only have about 65,000 lbs of fuel left. You can now step-climb to 41,000 feet and cruise here for the remainder of the flight. Some pilots like to fly fast and dirty in the first hour so they burn a lot of fuel and can climb to a higher altitude quicker. I think in the long-run, it helps save a lot of fuel because you can now cruise higher, and higher is usually better for fuel burn. Another factor is jet-stream winds. Generally when flying long-haul, you want to fly a route that the winds are the most favorable. This means when flying east-bound, you fly higher to ride the jet stream and fly faster. Flying west-bound, you want to fly lower, especially during winter when headwinds are really strong. I've cruised as low as 26,000 feet flying west-bound during winter time. I know this was not a weight issue because the flying time was only 5 hours on a Boeing 767. The return flight cruised at 41,000 feet to catch the winds. As a result, the flight times were different by more than two hours. So east-bound flights will generally fly higher than west-bound flights. Of course, weight issues are always present, and the end of a west-bound trans-pacific flight may cruise higher than an east-bound trans-pac that just departed. Other factors include ATC communications, other performance issues, or flight duration. On extremely short flights, you tend to not cruise as high because the high amount of cycles can really stress out the airframe. I know for a fact that Hawaiian Airlines likes their B717s to cruise between 12 and 24,000 feet on the inter-island flights. This is smart because fatigue is not as great. High-cycle aircraft tend to get a lot of stress, and it's smart to preserve these frames. Or if there are other aircraft at your preferred altitude, you'll just have to wait until they are out of the way. But that's probably a better idea, because if you hit someone else, the fuel burn savings won't help very much in lieu of a major airline disaster.

Question: Why is my AMS-MSP flight scheduled to take an hour longer than the return flight?
Answer: Flying westbound, you fly into the strong jet-streams of Earth. These winds are strong enough to influence travel time. Furthermore, these winds are usually stronger in winter time, I think due to the pressure differential caused by temperature fluctuations. Not sure how true this is, so someone might need to verify. But these winds can change travel times by more than an hour at times. I've flown from Honolulu to Japan in as long as 10 hours, but the return leg took only 6 hours. Flying towards Japan, our ground-speed was only 395 mph, due to a headwind of about 175mph. Flying towards Honolulu, the jetstream carried our 767 to speeds over 700mph. The 767 usually cruises at about 490 to 500 mph in still air, so you can see what a difference it made. In this case, the true airspeed remains at about 500mph. But the strong head or tailwind will change the ground-speed. So as far as the airplane is concerned, it's still flying at the same speed. A rule of thumb to remember is east-bound flights are usually faster by at least an hour than the same route going west-bound. Consequently, more fuel must be taken for a west-bound flight than an east-bound flight.

Question: Can a passenger airplane glide if all engines fail? If so, do planes with tail mounted jet engines also glide?
Answer: Yes, an airplane will glide if it loses all available power. The wings are there constantly providing lift, and even when experiencing a total loss of engine thrust, the wings will continue to provide lift unless they are destroyed. But let's assume the airplane is intact. I apologize for using a picture from the internet to prove my point, but let's say it's for educational purposes. When an airplane is in cruising flight, there is a constant balance of thrust, lift, weight, and drag that allows the airplane to maintain level flight. All these forces negate each other to allow the airplane to maintain a constant airspeed and a constant pitch. But when you lose all engines, now you don't have continuous thrust to negate the drag. The reason the airplane is in constant level flight is because all the forces equate to 0 when added up. But now, when experiencing a loss of thrust, the drag is now greater than the thrust being provided, which is now equal to 0. With the drag greater than the thrust, the airplane will start to slow down. Keep in mind that the lift and weight balance remain the same. It is true that the weight of an airplane changes during flight, but this happens over a long period of time, and with the engines not working, there is no fuel to be burned anyways. So let's say that all the variables remain the same except for thrust. When the plane slows down, the air moving across the wings won't be moving as quickly. It will be moving slower. There is now less lift to keep the plane in the air, and as a result, you have to descend. If you try to maintain level flight, you'll stall, and descend anyways. Consequently, the airplane will start to descend, because the balance of forces working against the airplane (thrust and weight) is greater than the forces working for the airplane (lift and thrust). The airplane will have to descend to maintain a constant pitch angle. But as it descends, it is still flying forward. It is slowing down, but it's still moving forwards. Essentially, the airplane is now gliding. Eventually, it will hit the ground, but for a Boeing 747 at cruising altitude, the glide ratio can be as much as 20:1, so the plane can glide for more than 100 miles. This will be enough for the plane to maybe find an airport to land at, or if not, it should be enough time to restart the engines. British Airways Flight 9 experienced a loss of all four engines, and it glided for many miles before restarting the engines. It did not fall out of the sky, contrary to what some movies may show. The only difference is that there will be next to no electrical power, so the cabin may get very stuffy and uncomfortable. But you won't crash for a while. You'll have a few minutes to think things over and maybe even land safely if you're lucky enough to be near an airport.

Question: Do pilots start the airplane's engines before reaching the runway?
Answer: Yes, pilots start the engines right after pushback from the gate or during push-back. It is standard practice to allow about a 5 minute period for the engine to warm up before taking off. You don't want to start the engines and accelerate them to takeoff power immediately. That's asking for trouble. Furthermore, starting the engines during push-back allows for more time to detect any unusual patterns or problems with the engines. If you started the engines right as you reached the runway, you may not notice that engine 1 oil temperature is high, or engine 2 is giving faulty readings.

Question: Does the Boeing 777 glide like the 747 once all its engines are shut down?
Answer: Yes it does. In fact, every airplane is able to glide, because when the engines quit, the wings are still there to provide lift to the airplane. The air is still flowing over the wings, the same way it was before the engines shut down, so the airplane won't fall out of the sky. It will be slowly coasting to Earth because no thrust to provide continuous lift, and depending on how high it is, can actually glide over 100km. Granted, a lot of systems will be lost because no engines means no electrical power, no bleed air to pressurize the cabin, etc. But the 777 has a lot of redundancy, and in the event of a total engine failure, there is a system called the RAT, short for ram-air turbine, to provide a little electrical power. The RAT provides some electrical power to give the pilot basic flight controls, and to display critical information such as airspeed, altitude, pitch, heading, etc. In the event the airplane loses both engines, the RAT will deploy. If there is fuel, the APU can also be used for a little electrical power. The only 777 that possibly experienced a double engine failure at cruise altitude was MH-370, after the airplane likely ran out of fuel. (BA 038 experienced a double engine failure at 500 feet). But we don't know how far MH 370 glided before hitting the water. However, the Airbus A330 has a glide ratio of 15:1, as seen in the Air Transat 236 incident, when the aeroplane experienced fuel starvation halfway across the ocean. Being of a similar weight and size to the A330, the 777's glide ratio is probably in this ballpark. This means that for every kilometer fallen, the 777 will travel 15 kilometers forward. So if at an altitude of 40,000 feet, or roughly 12 kilometers, you'll glide for up to 180 km. If you're somewhere over land, you'll probably have enough time to assess your options and maybe even find an airport to land at. So even if you lose all the propulsion to this airplane, you'll still be able to nurse it another 180 km. In short, the 777, like all other airplanes, is able to glide quite far if it loses all engines.

Question: Losing which part of an airliner would require an immediate emergency landing?
Answer: For a twin-engine airplane, losing an engine would be a big deal. Diversion to a nearby airfield would be recommended. CX 780 comes to mind, and BA 038 was another one. When discussing double engine failures, one must not forget the Gimli Glider or Air Transat 236. You'd be inclined to agree with me that if we lost an engine far away from land, you'd want to get to an airport soon. An incident I can think of was the United Boeing 777 flying from Auckland to Los Angeles. The airplane had to shut down an engine in cruise, and flew for more than three hours on one engine, eventually landing in Hilo, Hawaii. Vs a 4 engine airplane, an engine failure is a bigger deal on a twinjet. On 4 engines, it is not so critical, and I can remember a BA 747 crossing the entire Atlantic on 3 engines. This would never happen on a 777, because if you lose the other engine, you become fish-food. While it's extremely rare, it's better safe than sorry.

Question: Asiana Flight 214 Crash (July 2013): Were passengers evacuating the airplane allowed to take their carry-on baggage?

Question: Why can't a jetliner, like the 767, land with a full tank of fuel?
Answer: Number one, the aircraft was not designed to land at such a high weight because doing so will be impractical. Aircraft take-off at high weights because of all the fuel needed to fly long sectors. But after an 8-10 hour flight, most of this fuel is burned off, and the aeroplane is now much lighter, below the weight called a "maximum landing weight" which is what the aeroplane was designed to land at. Now, this normally works, but when there is an emergency that requires the airplane to divert immediately, he won't have time to burn off 10 hours of fuel. So the solution is to dump it. Every long range aircraft such as the 767, A330, A340, A350, A380, 747, 777, 787 can dump fuel. Furthermore, if something were to go wrong and the plane crashes, less fuel onboard means less fire. Or if the plane needs to do a go around, the climb performance will be better at a lighter weight. Overall, aeroplanes perform better at lighter weights, so this is something to consider as well. But in a grave emergency such as an inflight fire, the pilot may forgo the fuel dump and just land immediately. The airplane probably can handle an overweight landing but in these very rare cases, landing overweight is probably the least of the pilot's concerns

Question: Why do jets sometimes dump their fuel in-flight instead of waiting until they're on the ground?

Due to fuel being a large portion of this weight, aircraft are not designed to land at the MTOW of the aircraft because one would expect that on a 12-15 hour flight, a large portion of the fuel will be consumed. Fuel is a large percentage of the aircraft's weight on the beginning of a long trip, so the aircraft actually loses a lot of weight on a normal flight. However, in emergency scenarios after takeoff or in circumstances where the fuel cannot be burned, the fuel can be dumped to bring the aircraft back to its maximum landing weight. One might ask why the MLW is not the same as the MTOW. This is because it is too costly to build an aircraft to land at such a high weight (up to 573 tons for the A380) that 99 percent of the time will burn off the required amount of fuel to land at a safe weight.
